entry.title: BeeModel 0.24.0
entry.summary: The viewport on the GPU, issues VP1-VP5 (#363-#367): playing an animation in Solid, Material Preview and Rendered now keeps up at 2560 x 1440. docs/GPU.md; tools/playbench.py times it. Window frames a second while playing, on an RTX 4080 SUPER (v0.23.0 -> v0.24.0):
entry.content:
demoSolidMaterial PreviewRendered
dam break4 -> 1303 -> 1354 -> 71
rainstorm80 -> 18523 -> 18120 -> 27
leaf-twister77 -> 13145 -> 14445 -> 76
fireworks218 -> 21875 -> 214130 -> 169

Added

  • The 3D viewport drawn by the GPU helper (VP1, #363): Solid and Material Preview (shader graphs, textures, bump and normal maps, vertex colours, HDRI worlds) on a Vulkan graphics pipeline, each mesh's triangles kept on the GPU while it does not change; the colour, depth and object ids come back, so overlays, the outline and clicks work as before. The helper imports BeeModel's shared memory where the device can (VK_EXT_external_memory_host). BEEMODEL_GPU_VIEW=off keeps the CPU's viewport; edit and paint modes, virtualized geometry and light probes stay on the CPU. gpu(27..32).
  • Instances and particles in the same pass (VP2, #364): geometry-node and rigid-body instances and particle objects as instanced draws, points and sprites as quads made on the GPU. The rainstorm in Material Preview 46 -> 5 ms a frame.
  • Liquids solved on the GPU (VP3, #365): src/gpu/liq.comp, liquid.s's solver phase by phase (the dam break 67 -> 6 ms a frame); BEEMODEL_GPU_LIQUID=off, force fields and landscape colliders keep the CPU's. The viewport marches a liquid's field instead of meshing its surface. gpu(33..35).
  • tools/playbench.py: the demos played in the viewport at 2560 x 1440 in each shading (VP5, #367).

Changed

  • Rendered shading keeps up while playing (VP4, #366): the live view builds its scene as a render does (no CPU BVH with RTX, liquids as fields), fingerprints a liquid by its particles instead of meshing it, and no longer counts a slot's first allocation as build time (the dam break showed a still image until playback stopped).

Fixed

  • A liquid's surface was meshed every frame by the viewport's DAG scan, its wires' check and the live view's fingerprint even when nothing drew the mesh (30 ms each time in the dam break).
  • pt_stamp dropped the particles' step count, so the live view noticed a liquid's steps only through its re-meshed surface.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.23.0
entry.summary: Rendering performance, issues H1-H15 (#346-#360): every demo scene renders on the GPU, with RTX where there is one, and animations render faster. docs/GPU.md; tools/renderbench.py times it. A warm render at 960 x 540, 16 samples, on an RTX 4080 SUPER: rainstorm 1377 -> 103 ms, dam-break 1201 -> 63 ms, leaf-twister 313 -> 27 ms, fireworks 122 -> 24 ms.
entry.content:
Added

  • A render device setting (H1, #346): Properties › Render › Device and Preferences › System › Render device (render.device auto|rtx|gpu|cpu). Each render says where it ran and why ("Last render: on the CPU (a shadow catcher)"), in the Render panel, the Render area's header and the console; gpu(15..18).
  • On the GPU now, instead of the CPU: shadow catchers such as the Ground (H2, #347), HDRI worlds (H3, #348) and the Vertex Color node (H4, #349), each matching the CPU's image.
  • The GPU helper starts with the window and builds its kernels before the first render asks (H5, #350).
  • RTX (H10, #355): on a card with hardware ray tracing, renders and Rendered shading trace with ray queries; the images match the compute path's. Rainstorm frame: 165 -> 96 ms.
  • Motion blur from particle velocities (H11, #356): render.motion_blur <shutter> (Properties › Render › Motion blur): rain streaks.
  • Animation rendering (H12, #357): render_frames(folder [, first, last, w, h, samples, denoise]) and render.animation <folder> [first last]. The next frame is simulated and built while the GPU traces one: the rainstorm 109 -> 78 ms a frame. render.sh uses it.
  • Sample reuse between animation frames (H14, #359): render.sample_reuse <frames> (Properties › Render › Sample reuse). Later frames trace samples / (frames + 1) new samples and keep the frame before's where a pixel sees the same surface. A still scene with a panning camera at 16 samples and reuse 3 comes out closer to the reference than 16 new samples a frame, at a quarter of the cost. Moving objects keep only their own samples (the camera is reprojected, objects are not).

Changed

  • Particle balls are exact spheres, not 20-triangle balls (H6, #351): the rainstorm's scene build 1025 -> 206 ms.
  • BVHs are built on every thread (H7, #352), and each object keeps its own BVH between renders while it does not change (H8, #353): the rainstorm's BVH 949 -> 39 ms, its scene build on a third render 15 ms.
  • The scene stays on the GPU between renders (H9, #354): only the 4 KiB blocks that changed go up (a rainstorm frame sends 7.7 of its 100 MB).
  • A liquid's surface is traced on the GPU from its density field instead of being meshed every frame (H13, #358): the dam break 157 -> 109 ms a frame. It is still meshed for the viewport, CPU renders and exports.

Fixed

  • A new scene started with the last session's viewport cameras: a camera left far off made every new scene's viewport look empty.
  • The window's early helper start was ready too late again on a cold driver cache (about 7.5 s since the RTX kernels came): with RTX it no longer builds the compute path's graph kernel, which Auto never uses (ready in under 5 s).
  • Saving a partitioned world from the window crashed: the thumbnail taken first overwrote the path its cells were to be saved beside.
  • A saved file's Denoise setting was read back only when its sample count was large enough (the count was compared instead of the chunk's size).
  • After the scene stayed on the GPU (H9), particles growing within their buffer's spare room left the bytes after them unsent; with liquid fields read from there (H13) the GPU could lose its device (fireworks frame 107, then the CPU took over).

entry.title: BeeModel 0.22.1
entry.summary: Particle demos, a cache fix for keyed force fields, and the website.
entry.content:
Added

  • Particle demo scenes in Vibecoding/demos/: fireworks (chained died events, glowing through Vertex Color → Emission), dam-break (liquid, surface, foam, floating crates), leaf-twister (leaves drawn as objects in a keyed vortex) and rainstorm (hit events on a landscape and a roof, keyed wind).
  • The website (BeeModelHome/, beemodel.hideterms.com): features, a tour, the demo films, renders, downloads and every release's notes; now with particles and liquid and the four particle films.

Fixed

  • A force field moved by keys, or with a keyed strength, changed the simulation cache's key every frame, so particles and rigid bodies (and cloth, whose key mixes the same hash) simulated again from the start on each frame (leaf-twister reached 930 ms a frame; 60 balls 62 ms by frame 100). The key now takes such a field's animation instead of where it is and its strength now (fl_mix, an_fkeyed).

entry.title: BeeModel 0.22.0
entry.summary: Stage P of the 2.0 plan (Vibecoding/BeeModel-2.0-Plan.html): particles and liquid, issues P1-P7 (#337-#343). docs/PARTICLES.md.
entry.content:
Added

  • Particle systems (P1, #337): any object emits from its faces (by area), its volume, its vertices or its origin, at a rate between two frames (each particle moved on from its own moment of birth) or all at once, with a lifetime, a speed along the normal or a direction, a cone of spread, a size and a colour, each as random as asked (a hash of the seed and the id). Gravity, the force fields and drag; one step a frame, exact for a steady pull (a fountain follows the ballistic curve to 1e-3). Up to 4M particles in pooled blocks, stepped in parallel (1M in about 0.2 ms), the same on any number of threads. particles.add, particles.set, particles.remove; BeeScript emit() and particles(k, i). Systems undo, save (a PSYS chunk) and copy with a duplicate.
  • Drawing and rendering them (P2, #338): points, sprites (round, their size) or instances of up to 8 objects (at random or along their way), with the colour and the size changing over their life; 1M points draw in about 1 ms, the same picture on any number of threads. Renders show them as tinted balls or their objects; the GPU helper renders them the same (100k instanced leaves, tests/gpu.py).
  • Collisions and events (P3, #339): particles hit the Ground, landscapes, rigid bodies and cloth colliders (a segment cast a step: none passes through) and bounce, die, stick or split. Births, hits and deaths are events a second system is born of: rain that splashes, sparks that throw sparks.
  • Liquid (P4, #340): position-based fluids (src/liquid.s) with water, oil and honey viscosities, vorticity confinement and surface tension; a domain box and the Ground as walls, the scene's colliders, and moving rigid bodies pushed both ways (a light box floats, a heavy one sinks). A dam break of 200k particles runs at about 350 ms a frame on 8 threads; at rest the level is flat within one particle radius. from fill puts particles on a lattice inside the emitter.
  • The liquid's surface (P5, #341): meshed each frame (a smoothed density field, marching tetrahedra) into a closed, manifold surface that its emitter shows and renders, with the water material; spray where it breaks feeds foam; file.export_liquid writes an OBJ a frame. The dam break meshes in about 140 ms on 8 threads.
  • The Particles tab and presets (P6, #342): Add › Particles › Rain, Snow, Sparks, Confetti, Fountain, Water Tank; Properties › Particles (systems, Emission, Motion, Look, Collisions, Liquid, Cache with Bake and Free). The simulation cache keeps particles (channel 2) and liquids (channel 3), plays them back when scrubbing, bakes them (sim.bake particles liquid) and saves them with the file.

Fixed

  • Material Preview is no longer much slower than Solid on big meshes: each mesh's smooth corner normals are kept between frames (made again only when the mesh changes) and turned into the view in parallel - 31 ms to 3 ms a frame with a 127 000-face sphere.
  • A huge mesh (millions of triangles, e.g. an Array of a dense mesh) no longer clips the viewport: the triangles past ~5.6 million, and every object after them, were dropped (the triangle slots were capped by a 1 GiB frame arena; it reserves 16 GiB of address space now, used as touched).

entry.title: BeeModel 0.21.0
entry.summary: Stage A of the 2.0 plan (Vibecoding/BeeModel-2.0-Plan.html): attractors and force fields, issues A1-A6 (#329-#334). docs/FIELDS.md.
entry.content:
Added

  • Force field objects (A1, #329): Add › Force Field › Attractor (strength / distance squared, softened near its centre, or strength / distance; a negative strength pushes), Gravity Zone (a box or sphere whose down is its -Y), Wind (along its +X, with gusts), Vortex (turning round its +Y, with lift and inflow), Turbulence (curl noise) and Drag. Each has a falloff (none, radius, smooth), a strength that keys (field:Name:strength), the collision groups it acts on, and an on/off switch. They draw a gizmo of their kind and their reach. A Force Field section in Properties › Physics, field.add_<type> and field.set, BeeScript field() and force(x, y, z). Fields undo, save (a FLDS chunk) and copy with a duplicate.
  • Fields on everything (A2, #330): rigid bodies feel the sum at their centre of mass each substep (velocity first, so a circular orbit keeps its radius within 0.1% over ten turns); cloth and soft bodies per particle, with wind fields as air for each triangle. World › Gravity switches the world's gravity off for space scenes. Changing a field runs the simulation again (the cache's key).
  • Bodies that attract each other (A3, #331): Attracts the others on a rigid body (rigid.add attracts), G in World (rigid.world g). A Barnes-Hut octree once a step, the pulls across the workers, given as a leapfrog kick: two bodies orbit their common centre within 0.04%; 5445 attracting bodies run at about 500 steps a second (physbench nbody). rbinfo(22-24).
  • Walk on a planet (A4, #332): in play mode the player's up follows the pull where it stands and the camera turns with it, so walking round a sphere with an attractor brings you back to where you started. Logic nodes Set Strength and Field (the pull at a point). playinfo(16-18): the player's up.
  • Seeing the fields (A5, #333): View › Force Field Arrows (the pull on a grid round the fields) and View › Force Field Lines (streamlines from the selected objects). Presets Planet (a sphere with its core, the world's gravity off), Black Hole, Tornado and Breeze, also as field("tornado"). fieldinfo(k).

Fixed

  • A new armature's colour no longer comes from past the end of the per-type colour table.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.20.0
entry.summary: "UI round 2": the interface before the rest of the 2.0 plan (Vibecoding/BeeModel-UI2-Plan.html), issues W1-W11 (#317-#327).
entry.content:
Fixed

  • Picking a theme (#317): a dropdown inside a dialog (Preferences' Theme, UI scale, the AI provider ...) opened under the dialog and took clicks unseen. Lists are drawn over dialogs now. A theme picked from the View menu or the Viewport panel is kept in the preferences too.
  • The numeric keypad types values in fields, the console and the palette (#326).
  • The AI Assistant reaching its turn limit (error_max_turns, Claude Code or Grok CLI) now says so and how to go on ("continue" resumes the session), and the default limit is 100 turns (was 40).
  • Grok CLI no longer calls BeeModel's tools by their bare names (rejected as "not a valid MCP tool name"): its rules name them beemodel__... and say that a failed call does not mean BeeModel is disconnected.
  • The AI Assistant's transcript can be selected: drag over the text, or double-click a message; Ctrl+C or Copy copies just the selection (Copy with nothing selected still copies everything).
  • Rendered shading no longer flickers while an animation plays: it shows a raycast each frame until the scene holds still for 150 ms, then the path-traced samples.

Added

  • More themes (#318): Honey, Graphite, Nord, Solarized Dark, Solarized Light and Dracula, nine in all, each list showing a strip of every theme's colours.
  • A colour picker for every colour (#319): R G B and H S V numbers, the ten colours used last (kept) and the scene's own; copy, paste and reset on any colour field; the object colour and the paint colour form are swatches; an accent colour of your own for any theme.
  • A clearer Physics panel (#320): built from widgets in sections that fold (Rigid Body, Joints, Shatter, World, Cloth, Cloth World, the cache) under a status line. Type and shape before Add Rigid Body; dropdowns, units, start velocity and group; changes go to every selected body. Joints are listed and edited (type, the other body, pivot, axis, limits, motor, breaking force). Shatter gains seed, glue painting, the gap and the cut faces' colour; the cache says what is cached or baked.
  • A Landscape panel (#321): a Landscape tab for a landscape: size and samples; the layer stack with eyes, the picked layer's values, Add, Up, Down, Remove (landscape.layer up|down); paint layers with their colour, friction, bounce and rules; Add Sea, import, export, to mesh, tiles. Add › Water (landscape.add_water); the presets ask size, samples and seed; the sculpt shelf paints all eight materials.
  • A more powerful file dialog (#322): favourites, drives (mounted under /run/media, /media, /mnt, with their free space), recent folders (kept in ~/.config/beemodel/places), back and forward, the folder's parts as buttons, size and modified columns sorted by a click, a filter box, hidden files (Ctrl+H), all files, image previews.
  • Folders in the outliner (#323): nested groups that never move their objects, each with an eye, camera and lock for all inside; Ctrl+G, Move to Folder..., drag and drop, rename, fold; saved (FOLD) and undone; folder(), infolder(), folders(). Dragging a row shows a label at the pointer (what is dragged, what letting go does) and lights the row or folder that would take it (#327).
  • Reference images (#324): Add › Reference Image... (or a picture dropped on the window, or refimage()): square to the view, upright, drawn in every shading mode behind or in front of the scene, with an opacity, the sides it shows, and orthographic-only or square-on-only views; not rendered.
  • Demo scenes in Vibecoding/demos: a wrecking ball through a glued brick wall, exhibits that break on impact, a rockfall on an island; play.sh and render.sh (an MP4 through each demo's camera).

entry.title: BeeModel 0.19.0
entry.summary: "Shatter": stage S of the 2.0 plan (Vibecoding/BeeModel-2.0-Plan.html, planned as v1.2.0; released before stage D's v1.0.0), issues S1-S7 (#309-#315). How it works: docs/SHATTER.md, docs/PHYSICS.md; the benchmark: tools/physbench.py (shatter).
entry.content:
Added

  • Cutting a closed mesh into cells (#309): object.shatter. Each cell (a set of planes) is clipped from the mesh in doubles, and each plane's hole is filled at once, so every piece is closed. The holes are filled by bridging, ear clipping and merging back into convex polygons. A tree of cells cuts big meshes once near each cell, in parallel. Results: — the pieces' volumes add up to the original's within 1e-6, with no slivers; — 500 cells of a 49 000-triangle vase take about 54 ms; — an open mesh is repaired first. mesh.separate_loose (Mesh › Separate) splits a mesh into its loose parts.
  • The three patterns (#310): — shards: Voronoi cells from seeds inside the mesh, spread evenly, gathered around a point (at, cursor) or near the surface; — bricks: a running bond in the object's axes, set by size or counts, with offset, a mortar gap and jitter; — balls: packed on a face-centred cubic lattice inside the mesh, none overlapping. inner r g b colours the cut faces. Each piece keeps the original's material.
  • Every piece a rigid body (#311). Each piece is an active convex-hull body whose mass is its volume × the density (from density, else the material). Its centre of mass and inertia come from the hull itself. The pieces are children of the hidden original, and one undo step brings the original back. Piles of shards settle and sleep.
  • Glue (#312): glue N/m2 [paint]. A fixed joint ties every two pieces whose cut faces meet and breaks at the strength × the shared area. Joints now break inside the solve, so a 30 kg ball at 20 m/s knocks a hole the size of the ball in a glued brick wall and the rest stands. Up to 16 384 joints are allowed (ANIM v3 saves only those in use).
  • Shatter while it runs (#313): impact N s. The object stays whole until a blow that hard, then breaks in the same step, where it was hit. Its pieces are made and glued beforehand, so no frame takes over 16 ms. A logic graph's Shatter node breaks it on demand. The cache keeps which objects are broken. New rbinfo keys 17-21 report the fastest body, joint rows and impact groups.
  • The Shatter form and panel (#314): — Object › Physics › Shatter... opens a form that draws the cells as outlines on the object while it is open; — presets: Brick wall, Glass, Stone, Gravel balls (preset); — a Shatter section in Properties › Physics to re-cut with other settings (again); — BeeScript shatter(name, pattern, count [, options]), shinfo(k), get(name, "hidden"), and rigid(name, "x0") / "y0" / "z0".
  • tests/shatter.py checks all of it, the form and the panel with clicks in the fake compositor. tools/physbench.py times a 99 072-triangle vase cut into 500 shards: 455 / 163 / 121 / 105 ms on 1 / 4 / 8 / 32 threads.

Changed

  • Seeds and balls are tested inside the mesh through a grid of its triangles, as seen along the test ray: 250 ms became 12 ms on the 100 000-triangle vase.
  • Hidden objects are not rigid bodies, except originals that wait to shatter.
  • The joint list in Properties › Physics shows its first 6 joints.

Notes

  • Balls are not cut: they are spheres that fit inside the mesh, and the preview draws nothing for them.
  • A lone thin wedge-shaped shard can rock on the ground for a long time before it sleeps.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.18.0
entry.summary: "Ground and landscape": stage G of the 2.0 plan (Vibecoding/BeeModel-2.0-Plan.html, planned as v1.1.0; released before stage D's v1.0.0), issues G1-G7 (#301-#307). How it works: docs/LANDSCAPE.md, docs/PHYSICS.md; the benchmark: tools/physbench.py (mountain).
entry.content:
Added

  • The Ground (#301): Add › Ground (create.ground [height h]), an endless floor, one a scene. The viewport draws it as a grid that fades with the distance from the view's centre. Renders make it a shadow catcher: the film has alpha (no sky behind objects, the shadows caught on the ground); the render window shows it over checks, and render.save and render() write RGBA PNGs. It is a passive plane rigid body (friction 0.5), a cloth collider, and the player walks on it.
  • Landscapes (#302): Add › Landscape, landscape.add. A heightfield of 65 to 4097 samples a side over a chosen size, kept with its mesh (undo, copies, saving) and built from a stack of layers that stays editable: generate (fBm, ridged, billow, Voronoi cells), erode (droplets, then thermal), terrace, sculpted, flatten (round areas), heightmap; each with a strength, hidden or shown (landscape.layer add|set|remove|hide|show; landscape.set size|res|detail). A 1025 x 1025 landscape is generated and eroded in about 0.2 s, and a layer above the erosion changes in about 4 ms (the erosion's result is cached). landscape(name, k), height(name, x, z).
  • Sculpting and painting landscapes (#303). Sculpt mode on a landscape has its own tools, at its full resolution: raise, lower, smooth, flatten, ramp (a straight slope from where the stroke begins to where it ends), noise and erode, into a Sculpted layer; a stroke is one undo step. Paint layers (rock, grass, sand, snow, dirt, gravel, moss, mud: a colour, friction, bounce and a height and slope rule) are painted with clicks or by Auto Paint (rock on the slopes, grass on the flat ...); the blend shows in the viewport and in both path tracers. landscape.brush, landscape.paint.
  • The heightfield collider (#304). A landscape made a passive mesh body is not cut into triangles: each step, the cells under whatever moves become triangles on the fly, in slots kept while in use, and contacts work as on a mesh. Each paint layer has its own friction and bounce (a box slides further on rock than on grass). Cloth lands on landscapes by their heights. 1000 balls roll down a 4097 x 4097 mountain, none under its surface, 10 s simulated in 2.4 s.
  • Presets and water (#305): Add › Landscape › Flat, Hills, Mountains, Canyon, Dunes, Island. The island comes with its sea: a Water plane (the water material, rippled) that floats what is lighter than water - a wooden box floats, a stone one sinks - and that the player does not walk on. Generate gains island and offset. The welcome screen's Terrain template is a Hills landscape.
  • Heightmaps in and out (#306): landscape.import (16-bit or 8-bit PNG, grey or colour; OpenEXR scanlines, half or float, uncompressed or ZIP), landscape.export (16-bit grey PNG - a PNG made so round-trips exactly - float EXR, or the paint as RGBA PNGs), landscape.to_mesh [full], and landscape.tiles k, which splits a landscape into k x k landscapes that world partition streams (its cell files keep them as landscapes).
  • tests/landscape.py checks all of it (with clicks on the fake compositor for the brushes, the paint and the menus); tools/physbench.py times the mountain.

Notes

  • A landscape is drawn at up to 513 samples a side (every 2nd, 4th ... sample of a bigger one); the tile LOD drawing the plan names is not done.
  • Landscape painting lives in its sculpt mode's tools, not in Paint mode.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.17.0
entry.summary: "The solver": stage R of the 2.0 plan (Vibecoding/BeeModel-2.0-Plan.html), issues R1-R7 (#286-#292). How it works: docs/PHYSICS.md; the benchmark: tools/physbench.py.
entry.content:
Added

  • The rigid-body solver takes each step in substeps (#286, "soft step"): 4 by default (rigid.world substeps n, Properties › Physics › World › Substeps), with soft contacts that push overlaps apart as a damped spring (twice as stiff against static bodies) and a relax pass, restitution once at the end. Contacts between boxes and hulls are found by clipping their faces (src/clip.s): a box resting on another touches at its four corners. A tower of 20 boxes and a 10-layer brick pyramid stand (they used to topple), and a 100 kg box rests on a 1 kg one. tests/solver.py.
  • 10 000 rigid bodies (#287). Instances are bodies: rigid.add ... instances (Properties › Physics › Bodies) makes each instance of an object's geometry nodes a body shaped like its prototype; they move in the viewport and the renders, are baked into the cache and played back. Up to 4096 objects can be bodies (was 1024; files save only those in use and older files open). The broad phase is a hash grid, pairs are looked up in parallel in a hash kept between steps, and a big island's contacts are coloured and solved across the threads (the same result on any number of them). Contacts start further apart for fast bodies, so small ones no longer pass through each other; spheres collide exactly. 10 800 balls poured into a box: 10 s simulated in about 26 s on 8 threads (4000 took 23 s before); 5000 bricks settle at about 27 fps; 1000 tumbling boxes in 2.7 s (was 6.2). instpos(object, i, k); rbinfo(8..14).
  • Mesh and plane colliders (#288). A passive rigid body can be its mesh - any shape, each triangle a collider, found through a tree - or an endless plane (rigid.add passive mesh, passive plane; Properties › Physics › shape). Edges inside a flat surface don't catch: a contact there takes the face's normal, so a box slides over a ramp of thousands of triangles without a bump. Balls and boxes in a bowl, boxes on a staircase, 1000 balls on a terrain of 100 000 triangles at about 50 fps on 8 threads, a box landing on a plane 500 m out.
  • Fast bodies, groups and materials (#289). A body that moves more than half its size in a step is stopped short of static bodies by continuous collision, and contacts start as far apart as two bodies can close in a step: a 1 cm ball at 300 m/s and a tumbling box at 60 m/s stop at a 1 cm wall. Collision groups: rigid.add ... group n collide m (16 groups; m the groups it meets). Physics materials: material rubber|ice|wood|metal|stone and Properties › Physics › Material. A starting velocity: rigid.add ... velocity x y z.
  • Breakable joints, limits, motors and sliders (#290). rigid.joint ... break f breaks a joint whose load passes f newtons (it is gone for the rest of the run; rbinfo(15) counts them); limits lo hi stops a hinge (degrees) or a slider (metres) there; motor speed force turns a hinge (degrees a second) or moves a slider (metres a second) with at most that torque or force. A new slider joint keeps two bodies on a line, turning together (Add Joint › Type › Slider).
  • The same result on any number of threads (#291): 1000 tumbling boxes, 5000 bricks and the joint tests end bit for bit the same on 1, 4, 8 and 32 threads; rbinfo(16) hashes every body's state to show it.
  • The MIT License (LICENSE, also in the release archive). The 2.0 plan (Vibecoding/BeeModel-2.0-Plan.html): the masterplan's open questions, then physics - the solver, ground and landscapes, shatter, attractors, particles, smoke and fire.

Fixed

  • Rigid bodies: a body given an impulse when play began (Logic › Apply Impulse) did not move - the bodies were made again on the next frame. Continuous collision skips a body touching what it is checked against where its step began (it rests or slides on it).
  • Rigid bodies: a thin passive box (under 5 cm) was made 25 cm deep on every thin axis - meant for floors, it also thickened thin walls towards whatever came at them. Only a floor's own Y now; a passive body with no bounce no longer stops what comes at it short of it.
  • Sculpting: each thread's sums for a dab (the area's weight, centre and normal) get a cache line of their own. Two threads shared one, and how much that cost depended on where the linker put them (a brush frame took 4.1 ms instead of 2.6 when unrelated data moved).
  • parallel_for: a worker still leaving one call could take a chunk of the next - with the old chunk size, or past the old count - and part of it ran twice (a crash, or a different result, when many calls with different sizes ran back to back: the rigid-body steps). A chunk is now claimed by compare-and-swap on one word that holds the call's generation and the next index; the caller closes the last call's claim before it writes the next. The self-test runs 3000 calls back to back.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.16.0
entry.summary: "UI follow-ups": the parts of the UI plan (phase 11) left open at v0.12.0, issues F1-F18 (#267-#284; Vibecoding/BeeModel-UI-Plan.html, section Status), and Rendered shading.
entry.content:
Added

  • Text fields: Ctrl+Left / Right jump by word (Shift selects), Ctrl+Backspace / Delete remove a word.
  • File browser: Tab completes a folder or file name in the path field (a second Tab lists the matches); opening a scene shows a picture of it - saving from the window keeps a 192 x 120 picture of the 3D viewport in the .bee file (THMB, its first chunk).
  • Pie menus for the mode (hold Ctrl+Tab) and for the 3D cursor and snapping (hold Shift+S: Cursor to Selected, Selection to Cursor, Selection to Grid, Snap, Reset 3D Cursor - also in Object > Snap); a tap keeps the key's own action. mode.object / mode.edit / ... operators.
  • Context menus on fields (Reset to Default, Copy / Paste Value, Insert Keyframe, Copy Data Path), in the timeline (playback, Start / End at This Frame), the dope sheet and graph editor (interpolation, handles, duplicate, delete), and on files in the file browser (Open, Rename, Delete, New Folder, Copy Path); context menus show over dialogs.
  • The redo panel is made of widget fields: drag, type a value or an expression, an axis from a list.
  • The 3D viewport's header: View / Select / Object (Mesh) menus, a pivot point and orientation menu - Median Point, 3D Cursor, Individual Origins, Active Object; Global, Local, View, Normal (view.pivot, view.orientation) - which moves and turns follow, and an Overlays menu (grid, Text Info, Statistics, Navigation Gizmo, the mesh checks).
  • The navigation gizmo: drag a ball to orbit; zoom and pan handles under it; an orthographic view (Numpad 5, view.toggle_ortho).
  • Views glide to an axis, a reset camera or the new Frame Selected (Numpad .); Preferences > Interface > Reduce motion makes them jump.
  • Sculpting: brush falloff curves (smooth, sphere, root, sharp, linear, constant; sculpt.falloff), the dynamic-topology detail in the brush bar, and symmetry across Y and Z as well as X, in any combination (sculpt.symmetry xyz).
  • Status bar chips for long jobs - map, probe, lightmap and simulation bakes and imports - with their progress; the window keeps drawing while they run. A chip for the live link (click: the Versions editor).
  • CAD: reorder features in the feature tree (up / down buttons, cad.feature_move); a feature that now needs a later one is marked.
  • Print Check shows its findings in Properties > Object, each with a Show button that selects those edges or faces and frames them.
  • Outliner: a lock (viewport clicks pass through) and a camera (left out of renders) next to the eye; Ctrl+click toggles a row, Shift+click selects a range.
  • Parenting: Ctrl+P / Alt+P (Object > Parent), a Parent field in Properties > Object, the outliner as a tree (fold arrows, drag a row onto another). Children keep their world transforms and follow their parent's changes, whatever makes them; parents are kept in .bee files (PRNT). BeeScript parent(name), issel(name).
  • Lights: a type - point, sun, spot, area - and a size: a radius gives soft shadows, a sun its angle, an area light its edge; a spot's cone. Both path tracers sample them alike; the viewport draws each light's shape; Properties > Object and light.set type / size / angle.
  • Export Drawing (PDF) options: the sheet (A4, A3, A2, Letter; landscape or portrait), the views (front, top, right and an isometric view), the scale (fit, or 2:1 .. 1:100) and the title block's title and author, with today's date; drawing.options for scripts.
  • The welcome screen shows the version.
  • Scripts: scripts/build.sh, scripts/run.sh, scripts/package.sh (moved from the root) and scripts/deploy-omarchy.sh, which builds and installs BeeModel on Omarchy with its bar plugin (omarchy-plugin/).
  • Rendered shading: a fourth viewport shading, drawn on the GPU (the optional beemodel-gpu helper). While the view or the scene changes, one raycast a frame: the sun and point lights with hard shadows through the real BSDF, the sky with short-range occlusion and a rough first bounce, mirrors and glass followed. Once the view is still, Hive's path-traced samples accumulate on the GPU up to Preferences › Viewport › Rendered samples (64; 0 keeps the raycast alone), denoised on the GPU every frame (the F12 render's guided à-trous filter; Preferences › Viewport › Rendered denoise, view.rendered_denoise). The selection outline and the overlays stay on top. The scene goes up again only when it changes (a fingerprint of objects, mesh versions, lights, materials and undo steps); a slow-to-build scene waits for the change to end. An F12 render runs beside it. Without the helper Rendered shows Material Preview. In the header, the Z pie, View › Rendered, Properties › Viewport; view.shading_rendered, view.rendered_samples <n>, view.rendered_denoise [0|1]; gpu(7)..gpu(14). See docs/GPU.md.
  • The AI Assistant's Copy button (ai.copy): the whole conversation on the clipboard.
  • walkthrough16_ui: the new pieces driven with clicks and keys only: outliner Ctrl+click, Ctrl+P, the lock, a spot light, the snap pie, Numpad ., save and reopen with the scene's picture.

Fixed

  • A GPU render of a scene with nothing to render (every mesh hidden, left out of renders or deleted) after an earlier render could crash: the upload read the last scene's freed arrays. They are cleared when Hive lets them go.
  • The AI Assistant: a stream line longer than its buffer (an image from viewport_capture) is left out with a note instead of spilling base64 into the conversation; a result's later lines are indented.
  • BeeScript's "unexpected character" names the character, and explains that there are no lists for [ and ]; the AI's instructions say so too.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.15.0
entry.summary: Phase 14, "Blender files" (Vibecoding/BeeModel-Blend-Plan.html). BeeModel opens .blend files natively and saves them through Blender. The guide is docs/BLEND.md.
entry.content:
Added (Blender files)

  • The .blend reader (B1, #258): — both headers: the 12-byte one, and Blender 5's 17-byte one with 64-bit block lengths; — zstd files through the zstd program, gzip ones through BeeModel's inflate; — every field looked up by name in the file's DNA, with Blender's old names as alternatives; — pointers matched within the ID being read (Blender 5 numbers each ID's data on its own).
  • Meshes (B2, #259): all three layouts (MVert / MPoly / MLoop; CustomData layers in 3.4–4.x; AttributeStorage in 5.x). Positions, n-gons, the active UV map and material indices, checked against the file's block sizes.
  • Objects, cameras and lights (B3, #260): — the current scene's view layer, with excluded collections skipped; — world matrices from location, any rotation mode, scale, their deltas and the parent chain with its inverse, turned from Z up to Y up and taken apart into place, rotation and scale (baked into the mesh when it shears); — an object per material used; — camera lens and the scene's camera; — light colour and power.
  • Materials and images (B4, #261): Principled BSDF values. Image Texture nodes on base colour and emission, and a Normal Map node's image, become texture maps. Images come from the file (packed) or from beside it.
  • Import everywhere (B5, #262): — file.import_blend; — File › Import › Import Blender...; — the file browser's .blend filter; — files dropped on the window (text/uri-list over the Wayland data device): .blend, glTF, OBJ, STL and STEP are imported, and .bee opens when nothing is unsaved.
  • Export through Blender (B6, #263): file.export_blend and File › Export › Export Blender...: — glTF goes to a private folder, and Blender runs in the background (merge vertices, join triangles into quads, save); — a message says when it is saved, or shows Blender's error; — the Blender program is set in Preferences › Files; — the glTF export now writes cameras.
  • BeeScript get / set of a camera's lens and a light's power and colour (lr, lg, lb).
  • Tests (B7, #264): tests/blend.py, with fixtures and expected values from Blender 5.2 and 4.2 (zstd, plain and gzip). It covers the window's menu and drop, and runs an export round trip and a million-triangle import when Blender is installed.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.14.0
entry.summary: Phase 13, "AI first" (Vibecoding/BeeModel-AI-Plan.html): the AI comes inside the app. Describe a world, a model or a change, and an AI Assistant builds it in the scene through BeeModel's own tools, over Claude Code, the Grok CLI or OpenRouter. A real Preferences dialog holds every setting, connections included. The guide is docs/AI.md.
entry.content:
Added (AI first)

  • The Preferences dialog (A1, #246): Edit › Preferences and Ctrl+, open a modal dialog. It has a search across every category, eight categories (Interface, Viewport, Input, Keymap, Rendering, System, Files, AI) and Reset to Defaults per category. The Preferences area shows the same view.
  • More settings (A2, #247): the viewport's grid size, field of view and clip start; the default render resolution, samples and denoise. Each one is saved and applied.
  • AI connections (A3, #248): — the default connection; — Claude Code and Grok: program, model and turn limit; — OpenRouter: key, model, address and step limit; — text added to every request. The OpenRouter key is masked and kept only in ~/.config/beemodel/secrets (mode 0600), with OPENROUTER_API_KEY as the fallback.
  • Child processes and HTTPS (A4, #249): one child at a time. Its output is read from the main loop without waiting, and Stop ends it (TERM, then KILL). HTTPS goes through curl: the body and the key's header are in private files, never on a command line.
  • Claude Code (A5, #250): claude -p with stream-json, an MCP configuration naming beemodel --mcp-bridge for this instance, --strict-mcp-config --allowedTools mcp__beemodel, the turn limit and the instructions. Follow-ups use --resume.
  • Grok CLI (A6, #251): grok -p with streaming-messages-json. It runs in its own agent directory with a .grok/config.toml, which it loads because it runs with --trust. Its shell, file, sub-agent and web tools are turned off. Follow-ups use -r.
  • OpenRouter (A7, #252): chat completions with the curated MCP tools as functions (not the 600 single-operator tools). BeeModel runs each tool call in-process (mcp_local, under the same permission, undo and AI Activity as other agents) until the model answers or the step limit is reached.
  • The AI Assistant area and the AI workspace (A8, #253): — the connection picker, New, Revert, the transcript (text, tool calls, results, errors), the prompt (Enter sends), Send and Stop; — Ctrl+Shift+Space and AI › AI Assistant open it; the first time, they make the AI workspace (a viewport, the assistant, the outliner); — each request is one undo step, Agent: <prompt>; — ai.transcript prints the conversation. Preferences › AI has Test buttons for the three connections.
  • Prompt to world (A9, #254): the world-building instructions (the conventions, the look-plan-build-check loop, and BeeScript recipes for primitives, materials, terrain, scattering, lights and a camera) go with every request. They are also the MCP prompt build_world.
  • Tests (A10, #255): tests/ai.py runs Claude Code and Grok stand-ins and a localhost OpenRouter, with no network and no account.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.13.0
entry.summary: Phase 12, "PBR materials and a material editor" (Vibecoding/BeeModel-Materials-Plan.html): materials are physically based and driven by node graphs edited the way Unreal Engine's material editor works: a 42-node catalogue, a zoomable canvas with live previews, parameters and material instances, shared material functions, texture-set import, presets, baking to texture maps, glTF and OBJ texture exchange, and graphs on the GPU path tracer. The guide is docs/MATERIALS.md.
entry.content:
Added (PBR materials and material editor)

  • Material records v2 (M1, #228): materials grow to 4 KiB: graphs of 48 nodes, links that take a node's output 0..3, and a Material Output with 13 pins (base, metallic, specular, roughness, emission, opacity, normal, ambient occlusion, clear coat, coat roughness, transmission, IOR, opacity mask). Blend modes (opaque, masked, translucent), one-sided materials and the mask clip value, in the Material tab, matset and glTF (alphaMode, alphaCutoff, doubleSided). The path tracer lets rays and shadows through holes and translucent surfaces; the preview takes specular, IOR (F0) and AO from nodes. v0.12 files and .beea material assets open unchanged.
  • Node catalogue (M2, #229): 35 node types (from 9) with several outputs each: texture coordinate, position, normal, camera vector, vertex colour, time, constant, colour, Fresnel; vector math, separate, combine, mapping, panner, rotator; Voronoi, brick, wave, white noise, triplanar; hue / saturation, invert, brightness / contrast, desaturation, gamma, blackbody; 31 math operations; 11 mix modes; radial and spherical gradients. Texture Sample gives colour, R, G, B and alpha, reads images as colour (sRGB) or data, and repeats, clamps or mirrors. Node headers are coloured by category. nodeval() evaluates any node at a point.
  • Node canvas (M4, #231): zoom about the pointer with the text sized to match, Home / F to frame everything or the selection, box select, moving a whole selection, copy / paste (into other materials too), duplicate, cut, collapse (H), comment frames (C) that carry their nodes, reroute knots (double-click a wire), cutting wires (Alt+click, an Alt+drag knife), dropping a wire in empty space to add the node it feeds, wire colours by what they carry, align and distribute, a minimap and a right-click node menu. One undo step each.
  • Material editor (M5, #232): the add menu in a column per category with shortcuts that preset an operation (Add, Multiply, Lerp, Dot Product ...), a palette beside the canvas (search, click or drag to add), Unreal's quick keys (1, 3, T, U, A, M, D, E, L, O, N, P, B, then a click), the selected node's values as fields in the Material tab, a value clicked twice typed in the console, node.zoom, and Material Output pins the blend mode doesn't use dimmed.
  • Live previews (M6, #233): a preview pane with the material on a sphere, cube or plane (drag to turn, click for the next shape), a thumbnail of every node's output, and a stats line with warnings (nodes that lead nowhere, texture samples without an image). Each edit re-renders them within a frame: 9 ms for 24 nodes (budget 16 ms).
  • Parameters and material instances (M7, #234): Scalar, Vector and Texture Parameter nodes with names; material.instance (Material tab: New Instance) makes an instance that shares its parent's graph and values and overrides parameters (override boxes in the Material tab, matparam, material.param, material.param_reset); parent edits reach every instance, instances of instances work, parameters can be keyed (material:Blue:Wear), and everything is saved. 100 instances of one material render in one image, each with its own colour.
  • Texture sets and presets (M9, #236): material.import_textures (Material tab: Texture Set...) builds a PBR material from any one image of a texture set: its siblings are found by name (base colour, normal, roughness or gloss, metallic, AO, height, emission, opacity, packed ORM / ARM; _2k, _dx and the like understood) and wired through Texture Sample, Normal Map and Bump nodes. The Normal Map node reads DirectX (-Y) maps too. material.preset (Material tab: Preset...) gives a material one of 20 looks, from gold and glass to procedural wood, marble, concrete, fabric and leather.
  • Materials for scripts, agents and docs (M12, #239): MCP tools material_node_types (the catalogue), material_graph and material_graph_set (a graph as JSON, read and written; a loop or an unknown type is refused and nothing changes); scene_summary gives each node's place and parameter name. docs/MATERIALS.md describes the whole system; tests/materials.py walks through it (texture set, preset, baking, instances, a shared function, a masked leaf, the file and glTF).
  • Shader graphs on the GPU (M10, #237): the GPU path tracer evaluates material graphs (textures, patterns, math, mixes, bump and normal maps; a second kernel built only when a scene has graphs) and lets rays through masked, translucent and one-sided materials. A textured, bumped, normal-mapped and masked scene renders the CPU's image (99.8% of pixels identical); graphs with other nodes stay on the CPU.
  • Faster material graphs (M3, #230): each graph is compiled per edit: nodes that do not depend on the shading point (math, mixes, colours, parameters fed only by such nodes) are evaluated once and their results copied in; the Noise node runs its three channels four-wide (SSE, the same numbers as before); node dispatch is a table. A 40-node game-style material previews at about 2.2x a principled one while orbiting (was 3x); a heavy procedural one (noise, voronoi, wave, bump) at about 7.6x (was 10x). The path tracer renders the product shot 26% faster than v0.12. --selftest checks the four-wide noise and the folding on random graphs.
  • Material functions (M8, #235): a material function is a graph from Function Input nodes (In 1..3) to a Function Output (Out 1..3); a Material Function node runs it inline with its inputs, so one function can serve many materials and an edit to it reaches all of them. In the node editor, Ctrl+G turns the selected nodes into a function (links from outside become its inputs, what was used outside its outputs) and Tab on a Material Function node edits the function (Tab again: back). material.function_new, material.make_function; calls nest 8 deep.
  • Material baking, glTF and OBJ texture maps (M11, #238): material.bake <object> [size] [apply] (Material tab: Bake to Maps) bakes a material's node graph through the object's UVs into base colour, ORM, tangent-space normal and emissive maps; with apply the material samples them. glTF import reads TEXCOORD_0 and the five texture slots (base colour, metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion, emissive) with KHR_texture_transform, from GLB buffer views, data: URIs or files; export embeds the maps as PNGs, image graphs as they are and procedural ones baked. MTL gains map_Pr, map_Pm, map_Ke, norm / map_Bump and map_d both ways (-imfchan for packed maps). A helmet-style fixture round-trips with its textures, and Blender reads our maps.
