entry.title: BeeModel 0.11.0
entry.summary: Phase 10 of the masterplan, "Engine-grade & collaboration". BeeModel scales up and opens up to teams:
entry.content:
• Scale: cluster LOD DAGs (virtualized geometry) drawn through a new cut every frame, world partition streaming and a content library.
  • Play: play mode with walk and fly, logic graphs, light probes and lightmaps, and a live link that streams the scene over a socket.
  • Teams: versioned scenes (commit, branch, visual diff, three-way merge) and live CRDT co-editing for two users and an AI agent.
  • CAD: an exact B-rep / NURBS kernel and STEP import and export.
  • GPU: the optional beemodel-gpu helper path-traces and rasterizes on Vulkan, a second release asset; BeeModel itself still links nothing.

The exit checks: 1.05 billion source triangles fly at 5.8 ms a frame (median) in an 851 MB process (tests/billion.py, budget 8 GB); two users and an agent edit one scene and converge to identical documents (tests/coedit.py); STEP parts and assemblies round-trip through FreeCAD to 1e-6 (tests/step.py).

Added

  • Cluster LOD DAG (virtualized geometry, part 1, #143). vgeo.build turns the active mesh into meshlets: clusters of up to 128 triangles and 128 vertices, grown over their neighbours and seeded in Morton order. — Levels: each level groups neighbouring clusters, by shared edges and up to 1024 triangles, preferring edges across the old group borders so those get simplified too. Each group is simplified to half its triangles (area-weighted quadrics, half-edge collapses), with the group's border locked and no collapse that folds a pillow. It is then split into new clusters. This repeats until one cluster is left (a 1M-triangle sculpt: 14 levels, one root of ~120 triangles). — Errors: every cluster keeps its bounds and the error and LOD sphere of the group that made it and of its parents' group. Errors only grow up the DAG and the spheres nest, so any cut is crack-free. The self-test checks every level, 16 error thresholds and 24 cameras on a torus, a rippled 1M-triangle grid and 216 separate cubes. — Storage: one block, shared by the mesh's copies, saved in a VGEO chunk that starts on a page of the .bee file. In the window it is built on a background thread while the UI keeps drawing: about 120 ms per million triangles on 32 threads. Editing the mesh makes it out of date. — Operators and scripts: vgeo.extract <level | error> adds a cut as a mesh with its clusters coloured, vgeo.clear drops the DAG, and BeeScript's vgeo(name, k) reports on it.
  • Drawing cluster DAGs (virtualized geometry, part 2, #144). A mesh with a DAG is drawn through a new cut every frame (src/vgdraw.s). — Cuts: from the roots down, a group is refined while its error, projected from the camera, is over one pixel (vgeo.error). Each object is cut on its own thread; the chosen clusters are decoded into a mesh in the frame arena (64 clusters a job) and rasterized like any other. — Culling: a group whose LOD sphere is outside the frustum is skipped whole, and so is each cluster outside it. A cluster hidden behind last frame's depth pyramid (seen from last frame's camera) waits. After the first batch is drawn, the pyramid is built from this frame's depth, and the waiting clusters that are visible after all are drawn in a second batch. — Streaming: a DAG read from a .bee file stays mapped from it. Cluster data comes in 64 KiB pages, read ahead (madvise) when a group needs them and counted in once they are in memory. Past the budget (vgeo.budget, default 2 GB), the least recently used pages are given back; the roots' pages always stay. A group whose members are not in yet is drawn as the clusters it made, which keeps the cut crack-free. — Proxies: vgeo.proxy replaces the mesh, everywhere it is used, by its DAG's roots (welded), and the DAG goes with it. Files and memory then hold the DAG only. — The exit check: tests/billion.py builds 64 unique million-triangle terrain tiles and 8 boulders, places 960 linked copies (1.05 billion source triangles, a 2.1 GB file), reopens it and flies over it. Frames take 5.8 ms at the median (8.2 ms at the 95th percentile) on 32 threads. The process peaks at 851 MB, with 64 MB of pages under a small budget. — Tools: vgeo.view clusters | shaded | off | check (check: the drawn cut against level 0, for cracks), BeeScript vgstat(k) (the last frame's cut, culling and streaming) and view(yaw, pitch, distance, x, y, z) (the viewport camera). The zoom now goes out to 20 km.
  • World partition (#145). world.partition <cell size> [radius] splits a saved scene into grid cells on the ground (src/world.s). — Cells: plain mesh objects belong to the cell under them. Each cell is its own file beside the scene (<name>.cells/<x>_<z>.cell: meshes, UVs, colours, cluster DAGs and objects). The scene file keeps everything else and an index of the cells; on opening, the cells directory is read too. — Streaming: each pass of the main loop (and world.update in scripts) unloads cells past 1.25 x the radius, loads the cells in reach nearest first (two a pass) while the budget (world.budget) allows, and unloads the farthest while the budget is passed. — Edits: a fingerprint of each cell's objects tells a changed cell, which is written before it unloads. An object moved into a cell that is not loaded pulls that cell in, so objects cross borders. Saving writes the changed cells and keeps their objects out of the scene file; saving elsewhere copies the cells along. Streaming starts the undo history afresh (undo_clear). — Showing it: unloaded cells are drawn as boxes in the viewport, and a minimap (world.minimap) shows every cell (loaded, changed, on disk), the camera and its radius. BeeScript world(k) reports. — tests/world.py makes a 32 x 32 map of 4096 objects while partitioned (1024 cell files), flies over it under an 8 MB budget at ~3 ms a frame, edits on the way, and checks the edits after flying away, flying back, saving and opening again.
  • Content library (#146). The Asset Browser grows into a content browser over libraries of assets kept by their content (src/library.s). — Assets: lib.save object|rig|scene [name] [#tag ...] and lib.save material|tree|action <name>. Objects keep their meshes as evaluated, UVs, colours and cluster DAGs, with their materials saved as assets they depend on; rigs keep the armature, the skinned meshes and their weights; actions keep their curves; scenes are whole .bee files. — Content-addressed: each blob is blobs/<hash>.bee, named by a 64-bit hash of its bytes, so identical content is stored once. An asset's id hashes its kind, name, blob and dependencies. index.txt lists the assets; lib.add <folder> adds more libraries. — Placing: lib.place <asset> [x y z] (default: the 3D cursor) brings in dependencies first, places objects selected, rebinds rig meshes, and plays an action on the active object. Dragging a tile into a viewport places the asset on the surface under the pointer; a double click places it at the cursor. — Thumbnails: path-traced by a child process (beemodel --eval 'op("lib.thumbnail", id)'), one at a time, while the window goes on; lib.thumbnails makes them all now. — Finding things: tags (lib.tag Pillar #heavy -old), search (lib.search: every word in the name, kind or tags), dependencies (lib.deps, and the browser's uses / used by). — Packs: lib.pack <file.bee> [search] writes the matching assets and what they use: a manifest, each blob once, the thumbnails. lib.import checks each blob against its hash and adds only what is new. — Everywhere: every operation is an MCP tool (op_lib_*; packs and library folders need the agent's file permission). BeeScript gets lib(k), libfind(words, i) and libinfo(asset, what). tests/library.py checks the blob names against the hash, packs into a fresh library, background thumbnails, dropping into the viewport, and MCP.
  • Play mode (#147). F5 (play.start [walk|fly] [x y z]) snapshots the scene and plays it from the view (src/play.s). — Walking: a capsule (0.3 m radius, eyes at 1.6 m) under the rigid body world's gravity, in fixed 1/120 s steps against every mesh (a per-mesh grid of triangles, built on first use). It stands on slopes up to about 50 degrees and slides off steeper ones, is stopped by walls, climbs steps up to 0.4 m and keeps to the ground going down a slope. WASD moves, Shift runs, Space jumps; F switches to a fly camera (Space / C up and down). — Captured mouse: the pointer is locked (zwp_pointer_constraints_v1) and its relative motion (zwp_relative_pointer_v1) turns the view; the cursor is hidden. — Live scene: the frame runs on in real time, so rigid bodies, cloth, keyed animation and rigs play while you walk. — Leaving: Esc frees the mouse and asks: K keeps what happened as one undo step, D (or Esc) discards it, the scene, the frame and the view as they were. play.stop [keep|discard] does the same from scripts. — Scripted: every operation is an MCP tool (op_play_start, op_play_stop, op_play_mode); BeeScript gets playstep(seconds, forward, right, up, run), playlook(yaw, pitch) and playinfo(k). tests/play.py walks a small level (walls, stairs, a ramp, a slope too steep, falling boxes, a keyed spinner) and plays it in a window with keys, mouse motion and MCP. — run_op gives every operator an aligned stack, whoever calls it (keys, MCP, scripts).
  • Logic graphs (#148). Event nodes that run in play mode (src/logic.s), edited in the node editor like the other graphs. — Nodes: events (Begin Play, On Tick, On Key, On Overlap, On Hit, On Timer, On Message), actions (Move, Rotate, Set Property, Spawn, Destroy, Play Action, Apply Impulse, Set Visibility, Send Message, Set Variable, Branch) and data (Variable, Math with 18 operations, Info: time, location, the player, distance, random..., Get Property). Run inputs chain actions after the event or action before them; names (messages, objects, properties, actions) are kept in the graph. — Attached: logic.new, logic.node, logic.name, logic.attach (a Logic modifier on the object); links and values with tree.link / tree.node_set. Graphs are node trees, so they are saved in the .bee file and undone like the rest. — The VM: every fixed play step (1/120 s) runs each object's graph in a fixed order, then delivers the messages sent. It is deterministic (random is a hash of the step, node and object) and sandboxed: 4096 nodes a step (the rest of the step is skipped), 256 messages a step, 256 spawns, objects only by name. — Play mode around it: the player rides what it stands on (moving platforms), contacts report hits, the rigid body world runs live (no cached frames) and takes impulses, scripted playstep advances in 1/60 s frames as the window does, and playkey(code, down) presses keys. An action layer that has played out now holds its last pose. — Hidden objects: object.hide (H) and object.reveal (Alt+H); hidden objects are not drawn, rendered, picked or collided with. Destroy and Set Visibility use the same flag. — The node editor shows an object's logic graph (before its geometry tree; Tab: the material): red events, green actions, blue data, white run sockets; Shift+A lists the logic nodes; pressing a name value puts logic.name ... in the console to finish. — tests/logic.py: a door that opens, a pickup that is counted, a spawn on E, a pushed ball, a moving platform; saved and opened again, run twice to the same result, a message storm cut off at the budget; the node editor, F5 and MCP in a window.
  • Lighting tools (#149): light probes, a lightmap baker, glTF for engines. — Light probes (src/probe.s): probe.add irradiance|reflection [x y z] [half size] [grid points], probe.bake [rays]. Irradiance volumes keep a grid of L2 spherical harmonics (convolved with the cosine lobe), reflection probes a 6 x 32 x 32 cube map; both are baked by the path tracer (a new trace_ray: a path from any point along any direction) in parallel. The material preview takes its diffuse light from the smallest volume around a point (trilinear) and its reflections from a reflection probe's box (box-projected); where a volume lights it, the studio softboxes are left out. The probes are drawn as boxes in the viewport, kept in undo and saved (PRBE). — Lightmaps (src/lightmap.s): lightmap.bake [size] [rays] gives every visible mesh a second UV set (a smart projection of a copy, packed), places the objects in one atlas by their area, traces the irradiance at every covered texel (cosine-weighted, from just above the surface), denoises (a-trous, normal, distance and luminance weights) and dilates; lightmap.save writes OpenEXR or PNG. Saved in the .bee file (LMAP), not in undo. — glTF for engines: light objects as KHR_lights_punctual; a baked lightmap as an embedded PNG, the second UVs as TEXCOORD_1 and a material per lightmapped object with MOZ_lightmap whose KHR_texture_transform is the object's atlas region; KHR_materials_emissive_strength as before. — BeeScript: probe(k), probeinfo(n, what), probesample(...) (the probes, or irradiance traced directly as the reference), lightmap(k), lmsample(object, x, y, z, c). — tests/lighting.py: probes and the lightmap checked against traced irradiance (shade, colour bleeding, reflections), undo, saving, PNG and EXR, the export through the Khronos glTF validator (no errors, no warnings), the preview lit by the probes.
  • Live link (#150): the scene streamed over a socket (src/link.s). — link.serve [port] | lan [port] | unix:<path> serves a versioned binary stream: HELLO, a snapshot (materials, meshes, objects), then the changes - OBJECT, DELETE, TRANSFORM, PROPERTY (name, material, hidden, colour), MESH, MESH_DELTA (only the runs of vertices that moved), MATERIAL - each turn of the event loop after a TICK with the editor's clock. Changes are found by comparing the scene with what was sent. — beemodel --link host:port (or link.connect) mirrors a session; docs/LIVELINK.md documents the protocol for engine plugins and tools/livelink.py is a reference reader. — Under a millisecond on localhost; a reader that falls behind gets its transforms coalesced (one, the latest, per object once it catches up). — tests/livelink.py: snapshot, latency, deltas, topology changes, a mirror, backpressure, a late reader, a UNIX socket.
  • Versioned scenes (#151): commit, branch, diff and merge .bee files (src/vc.s). — History: beside the saved file, <file>.vc/ keeps content-addressed blobs (whole scenes, each object's mesh, manifests: an entry per object and a hash per mergeable chunk), commits (text: scene, manifest, parents, time, message; named by their hash) and the branches. vc.commit [message], vc.branch, vc.switch (refused with changes unless force), vc.log. — Visual diff: vc.diff [branch | commit] [overlay | side] lists objects added, removed and changed (which properties; meshes with their vertex counts) in a panel and on the console, and draws the other version as ghosts - over the scene or beside it. — Three-way merge: vc.merge <branch> from the common ancestor, per object and property (transform, name, material, hidden, colour, mesh) and per chunk (materials, node trees, animation, light probes): one side's change is taken, different changes to the same thing are conflicts for the merge panel (ours / theirs buttons, vc.resolve); vc.commit makes the merge commit (two parents), vc.abort gives up. — Every operation is an MCP tool: an agent can branch, work and propose its branch for the user to diff and merge. BeeScript: vcinfo(k), vctext(what, row). — tests/versions.py: commits, branches, the diff, merges with and without conflicts, the store, the panel's buttons, ghosts over and beside the scene, an agent's branch over MCP.
  • Live co-editing (#152): two users and an AI agent on one scene (src/cosync.s, src/cotree.s). — co.host [port] starts a session, co.join host:port joins any of its peers (co.host on a peer in a session lets others join there too); operations are relayed peer to peer, each kept once - no server. — The CRDT: objects are elements with unique ids (alive by their latest add / delete, in an RGA sequence for the object list); name, material, transform, hidden and colour are last-writer-wins registers (Lamport clock, the peer below); a mesh is a topology generation plus a position register per vertex (moves of different vertices merge); materials are registers by name; node trees are a set by name with their nodes in an RGA sequence (content and links by node id one register each). — Edits of any kind become operations by comparing the scene with the document every turn of the event loop; remote operations update the document, then the scene. — Undo per author: Ctrl+Z in a session undoes your own last edit (as new operations: others' later edits stay); redo likewise. — The agent: co.agent on makes what MCP tools change a peer of its own, with its own undo and presence (the objects it last touched). — Presence: every peer's camera, 3D cursor and selection are drawn in its colour; co.follow <peer> keeps your view on theirs. — The co-editing messages are in docs/LIVELINK.md. BeeScript: costat(k), cohash() (the document's hash), plus viewinfo(k) and objtype(object). — tests/coedit.py: three peers in a chain (one the agent): joining, concurrent edits of one property, vertex merges, node graphs edited at once, per-author undo and redo, presence and follow, and a fuzz of hundreds of random concurrent edits converging to identical documents (by hash) and scenes.
  • The B-rep kernel (#153): cad.kernel on makes CAD features build exact solids instead of meshes (docs/BREP.md). The switch is saved with the scene. — Geometry: - Curves are lines, circles, ellipses or NURBS; surfaces are planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, tori or rational NURBS, all in the STEP parametrisations. - NURBS evaluation with derivatives, knot insertion, and degree elevation of curves and surfaces. — Topology: - Bodies, faces trimmed by loops, coedges with pcurves, edges and vertices. - Volume and area are integrated exactly over the trimmed faces (Green's theorem in (u, v)). — Solids from sketches: pads, pockets, holes, shells and revolves are built from the sketches' exact lines and arcs, with patches of at most half a turn and poles on the axis. — Booleans: - The surface-surface intersection is in closed form for the plane / quadric cases and traced (marching squares, Newton onto both surfaces) otherwise. - Each face is divided in (u, v) and its regions classified; coplanar, tangent and along-edge contacts are handled. — Fillets and chamfers: straight edges between two planes. — Tessellation: adaptive, watertight and Delaunay in the surfaces' metric; it is what the viewport shows. — A body the kernel cannot build (e.g. infill, or fillets meeting at a corner) keeps the mesh replay's result. — BeeScript: brep(name, what) and nurbscheck(k). — tests/brep.py checks: - the NURBS self-checks; - closed-form volumes and areas of pads and revolves, to about 1e-15; - booleans: a hole drilled across a rod against an independent integral (3e-8); - fillets and chamfers; - the enclosure walkthrough on the kernel, before and after a parameter change: valid and watertight; - the switch in saved files.
  • STEP import and export (#154), our own Part 21 reader and writer (docs/BREP.md): — file.export_step writes B-rep solids as AP214: - geometry: planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, tori, B-spline surfaces and curves, rational or not; - one part in place, or several as an assembly with their placements; - each solid's name and colour, and the scene's units (millimetres, centimetres, metres, inches). — file.import_step reads parts and assemblies: - analytic or NURBS faces, seams and poles; - placements through every level, names, colours, and the file's units converted to the scene's. - Imported solids are kernel bodies, so brep() and the export see them. — BeeScript's get and set take "color". — tests/step.py checks: - our own round trip: volumes and areas to 1e-9 (about 1e-15 seen), placements, colours and units; - FreeCAD (or OpenCASCADE) reading our part and assembly (volumes to 1e-6, each solid in place); - its re-export, and its every-face-NURBS version, read back to 1e-6. — CI installs FreeCAD from its PPA for the round trips.
  • The GPU helper (#155): beemodel-gpu, an optional second program and release asset, links the Vulkan loader. BeeModel still links nothing and talks to it over a socket and shared memory (docs/GPU.md). — Path tracing: Hive's samples run on the GPU. The shader is a line-for-line port with the same random streams, so the images agree with the CPU's: the default scene is pixel-identical, and a scene of glass, metal, clearcoat and lights differs by 0.01 levels on average. 128 samples at 1080p take 0.9 s on an RTX 4080 SUPER, against 9.8 s on 32 CPU threads. — Rasterization: for frames drawn through cluster DAGs, the viewport rasterizer's tile stage runs on the GPU, pixel-identical to the CPU. — Fallback: without the helper, without a usable device, for scenes the GPU kernels do not cover (an HDRI world, shader graphs), or if the helper fails mid-render, the CPU paths go on from where they were. — Choice of device: a discrete GPU first, then an integrated or virtual one; llvmpipe only with BEEMODEL_GPU=any. BEEMODEL_GPU=off turns it off, and BeeScript's gpu(k) reports on it. — tests/gpu.py checks the fallbacks, the path tracer against the CPU (also denoised), the helper dying mid-render, and the rasterized frame; CI runs it on llvmpipe.
  • Job system: parallel_for is shared by the UI thread and one background thread (job_spawn), which take turns.

Fixed

  • modapply in a script gave its scratch memory back only at the end of the script: a script applying many large geometry node modifiers ran out of frame memory (a flat result, then a crash).
  • Leaving sculpt mode now marks the mesh as changed, so caches keyed by its version see the strokes.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.10.0
entry.summary: Phase 9 of the masterplan, "Animation & simulation". Scenes move:
entry.content:
• Keyframes: Bezier, linear and constant F-curves on anything a script can set, with a timeline, a dope sheet, a graph editor and action layers.
  • Rigging: armatures with automatic (bone heat) weights, linear blend and dual quaternion skinning, pose and weight paint modes, constraints, IK (FABRIK / CCD, poles), drivers, shape keys, motion paths and onion skins.
  • Mechanisms: CAD parts on revolute and slider joints, gears and racks, limits and collision checks, driven by keyed parameters.
  • Rigid bodies: boxes, spheres, capsules, hulls and convex compounds with GJK / EPA contacts, persistent manifolds, islands solved in parallel, sleeping and joints, set up from a Physics panel.
  • Cloth and soft bodies (XPBD): pins, colliders, self collision, wind and volume, with coloured constraint batches solved in parallel.
  • Simulation cache: frames kept and played back, bakes saved in the file, invalidated by edits.

The exit checks:

  • **tools/fakewl.py:** 1000 boxes tumbling into a heap simulate 10 s in less than 10 s.
  • **tests/animation.bees:** builds a character (a 178,656-vertex SDF body skinned to a 12-bone armature, IK legs on keyed feet: a walk cycle), a gear pair turned by a keyed parameter, 1000 rigid boxes and a draping tablecloth. It bakes 10 s, saves and renders three frames. tests/animation.py checks the numbers and the reopened bake, then plays the saved scene in a window: each frame stepped in under 16.7 ms (60 fps).

Benchmark on a 32-thread desktop (Ryzen 9 7950X):

  • The rigged character: a played frame of the whole walkthrough scene (keys, IK, skinning 178k vertices, the mechanism, the baked bodies and cloth) evaluates in 7.0 ms; in the window, stepped and drawn, 10.1 ms at the median.
  • 1000 rigid boxes: 10 s simulated in 5.9 s (4 threads: 6.7 s; 1 thread: 8.2 s). Baked with the cloth and the rig over 239 frames in 9.0 s, then scrubbed back at 3.1 ms a frame.
  • Cloth: a 6561-particle sheet colliding with a ball, the floor and itself simulates 4 s in 3.0 s.
  • Animation walkthrough: 16.7 s end to end, three 480x270 frames rendered in 0.9 s.

Added

  • The simulation cache: — Cached frames: rigid bodies and cloth keep each whole frame as the simulation reaches it. Scrubbing back plays the cached frames instead of simulating again, and the scene's start keeps them. Cloth vertices are stored as 16 bits a coordinate within each cloth's bounds (half the memory; within 0.2 mm on a 2 m flag). — Invalidation: the cache belongs to a key made from the settings, pins, the objects' start places and meshes, and the animation (keys, layers, drivers, constraints, mechanism joints). An edit that changes the key drops it, and the simulation starts again. — Bake: sim.bake [rigid|cloth] simulates the frame range and keeps it whatever changes until sim.free [rigid|cloth]. A baked cache is saved in the .bee file (SIMC), and past its end it holds the last frame. — Memory: all channels share a budget (sim.cache budget MB, 1024 MB by default); a channel that would go over it stops recording. sim.cache reports what is held. — Timeline: a line under the ruler shows the cached frames, brighter when baked. — Speed: 1000 boxes scrub back at under 2 ms a frame from a 6.4 MB cache of 239 frames. — BeeScript: cacheinfo(k).
  • Keyframes and the timeline: — Keys: anything a script can set can be keyed: object transforms, material values, modifier parameters, node inputs and values. — F-curves: Bezier with auto-clamped handles (flat at extremes, never overshooting), linear or constant interpolation. — Keys in the window: I keys the selected objects' location, rotation and scale at the frame; Alt+I removes those keys. — Frames: setting a frame shows the scene there. Space plays (looping over the frame range at the scene's fps), Left / Right step, Shift+Left / Right jump to the ends. — Timeline area: shows the frame, the range, the ticks and the selected objects' keys; dragging in it scrubs. — Storage: keys and the range are saved in .bee files (ANIM) and undo with the scene. — Operators: anim.* (insert_key, delete_key, key, unkey, frame, play, range, interpolation).
  • Armatures and skinning: — Armatures: bones (rest head, tail and roll, parents, joined chains) and poses (location, Euler rotation, scale in the bone's axes). Create > Armature, arm.bone, arm.pose. — Armature edit mode (Tab): click joints, G / R / S, E extrudes a joined bone, X deletes (skin weights follow). — Pose mode (Ctrl+Tab): click bones, G / R / S in their own frames, I keys them, Alt+R clears. Bone poses are animation channels (bone:Rig:Upper:rz). — Armature modifier: deforms a mesh by four weights a vertex, with linear blend or dual quaternion skinning, in parallel. — Automatic weights: by bone heat: each bone's heat equation is solved on the mesh, and the four strongest bones are kept. arm.parent <mesh> <armature> sets up both. — Weight paint (Ctrl+W): paints the active bone's weights, shown as a heat map. paint.weight sets the value; BeeScript has wpaint. — BeeScript: armature, bones, weight, evpos. Bones are saved in ARMT and weights in MWGT.
  • Cloth and soft bodies (XPBD): — Objects: cloth.add [cloth|soft|collider] [stretch c] [bend c] [volume c] [mass m] [damping d] [thickness t] [friction f] [self] on the selected meshes. Compliances are in m/N; 0 is stiff. — Constraints: stretch on every triangle edge; bend between the far corners of triangles sharing an edge; a soft body's closed mesh also keeps its volume. Constraints are coloured into batches with no shared particle, and big batches are solved in parallel. — Pins: cloth.pin selected | all | none | above <axis> <value> | below <axis> <value> sets a mesh's pin group (saved in MPIN). Pinned vertices hold to the object as it moves. — Collisions: cloth keeps its thickness from collider objects' triangles (a spatial hash; very large triangles are checked by every particle) with friction. With self it also keeps off itself and other self-colliding cloth (a particle hash; rest neighbours are left out), resolved in parallel. — Forces: gravity (the physics world's) and wind as drag on each triangle (cloth.world wind x y z). Each step (60 a second) is cut into 10 substeps (cloth.world substeps n rate n). — Timeline: like rigid bodies it runs from the scene's start; while it runs an object shows its simulated mesh. — Speed: a 6561-particle sheet colliding with a ball, the floor and itself simulates 4 s in 3.0 s. — BeeScript: clothinfo(k).
  • Mechanisms for CAD assemblies: — Joints: mech.joint <revolute|slider> <part> <parent|world> [pivot x y z] [axis x y z] moves a part about or along an axis, relative to its parent part. The part as it is when joined is its place at 0. Parts can be chained: an arm on a gear turns with it. — Values: a joint is driven by an expression of CAD parameters, units and frame (value angle, value crank * 2, value frame * 3deg), or by another joint times a ratio (gear 1 -2 for a gear pair; a slider from a revolute joint is a rack). min / max limits hold it, and it says when it is held. Also mech.set, mech.remove, mech.list. — Parameters animate: CAD parameters are animation channels (param:angle), so a keyed parameter moves the whole mechanism over the timeline and rebuilds the sketches and features that use it. — Collisions: after the parts move, each moving part is checked against every other mesh. A triangle edge passing strictly through the other part counts; touching faces do not. A pair that starts colliding is reported in the console. mech.check lists them now. — BeeScript: joint(n [, 1]) reads a joint's value, or whether it is held at a limit; collisions() counts the colliding pairs.
  • Rigid body physics: — Bodies: rigid.add [active|passive] [box|sphere|capsule|hull|compound] [mass m] [friction f] [bounce b] [damping d] on the selected objects. Active bodies fall and collide; passive ones are collided with. A thin passive box (a ground plane) gets depth below its top. — Shapes: a box, sphere or capsule; the mesh's convex hull; or a compound, where the mesh is cut into up to 16 convex parts until each is close to its hull (a ball drops through a torus's hole). — Collision: sweep and prune, then GJK and EPA on the parts. Contact manifolds of up to four points are kept between steps; for boxes and hulls more points are found by tilting one shape about the contact. — Solver: sequential impulses with warm starting, friction, restitution, speculative contacts and Baumgarte correction (overlaps part at most 1 m/s). Islands of touching or jointed bodies are solved in parallel, and an island at rest for half a second sleeps. — Joints: rigid.joint <fixed|hinge|point> <object> <object|world> [pivot x y z] [axis x y z]. rigid.world sets gravity, the step rate (120 a second) and iterations (10). — Timeline: the simulation runs as the frame passes the scene's start, from where the objects are there. Going back to the start puts them back. Settings are saved with the scene. — Speed: 1000 boxes tumbling into a heap simulate 10 s in 6.2 s on a 32-thread desktop; the slowest frame takes 34 ms of the 41.7 ms a 24 fps frame allows. On 4 threads it takes 6.7 s. — Physics panel: the Properties area has a Physics section for the active mesh. + Rigid Body makes it a body. Buttons switch Active / Passive and step through the shapes. Mass, friction, bounce and damping are fields you drag. Its joints are listed with x to remove them, followed by the world's gravity, steps a second and iterations, and a line on what the simulation is doing while it plays. x removes the body. — BeeScript: rigid(name, prop) reads a body's type, shape, mass, friction, bounce or damping; rbinfo(k) reports bodies, contact points, awake bodies, islands, frame time, manifolds, steps and parts.
  • Rigging: — Object constraints: copy location / rotation / scale (chosen axes, optionally added to the object's own), track to (an axis at the target, another up), limit location / rotation / scale, child of. Each has an influence and can be muted. They work on the object's own transform, so moving or keying a constrained object still works. constraint.add, constraint.remove, constraint.set, constraint.list. — IK: a bone's chain (any length) reaches for a target object, by FABRIK or CCD, and bends towards an optional pole object. The rest of the armature and skinned meshes follow, and so does dragging the target. constraint.add Rig:Hand ik Goal chain 2 pole Knee. — Drivers: a property set by an expression (with units and functions) of named other properties and frame, e.g. anim.driver Door:ry a=Handle:rz a*2. Any animation path can be driven or drive. — Shape keys: relative to the Basis, mixed before the modifiers. shape.add Smile stores the mesh as a key; edit, then shape.add Smile again stores the edit and brings the Basis back. Values (shape:Cube:Smile) can be keyed and driven. Saved in MSHK; constraints and drivers are saved with the animation. — Motion paths: the selected objects' (in pose mode, the selected bones') paths over the frame range, with a dot a frame and larger dots at keys. anim.motion_paths. — Onion skins: the active object a few frames before (red) and after (green), as wires that follow playback. anim.onion 2 2 4. — BeeScript: prop(path) (any property by its animation path), bonepos, shapes.
  • Dope Sheet, Graph Editor and action layers: — Dope Sheet: a row of keys for each curve. Click selects (Shift adds), a drag moves the selected keys by whole frames, Shift+D copies them ten frames on, X deletes, A selects all or none. — Graph Editor: every curve fitted to the view, with a selected key's Bezier handles. Dragging a key moves it in frame and value; dragging a handle shapes it and makes it free. — Key operators: anim.select_keys, move_keys, scale_keys, duplicate_keys, delete_keys, handle_type, handle. — Actions: anim.action <name> keeps the selected objects' keys as a clip. anim.layer <action> [object] [start] [influence] [replace|add] [repeat] plays it on top of the scene, NLA-style, and layer_set / layer_remove change layers. Actions and layers are saved in the ANIM chunk. BeeScript: frame, key, unkey, keyed, with paths like "Cube:x", "material:Red:roughness", "modifier:Cube:0:levels" and "node:Tree:3:5".

entry.title: BeeModel 0.9.0
entry.summary: Phase 8 of the masterplan, "Nodes & procedural". BeeModel builds geometry from node graphs:
entry.content:
• Node editor: shader graphs and geometry node trees as boxes and wires, with groups and an asset library.
  • Geometry nodes: 39 node types run by a Geometry Nodes modifier. Their fields compile to a block-vectorized VM, and a template JIT turns hot programs into AVX / SSE machine code.
  • Scattering and instancing: a million instances, placed in milliseconds and drawn without being realized.
  • Curves: Bezier and poly splines, edited in a curve edit mode and swept into tubes or along profiles, plus curve nodes.
  • Generators: terrain with erosion, L-systems and wave function collapse.
  • Procedural co-pilot: AI agents build node setups as proposals that the user accepts or reverts in one step.

The exit checks:

  • **tools/fakewl.py (instancing):** places a million instances in under 200 ms and orbits 100k of them in the window.
  • **tests/procedural.bees:** builds an eroded valley with scattered rocks and L-system plants from one tree, a curve rail with posts from a second, and a meadow of a million instances from a third. It saves and renders the scene. tests/procedural.py checks the numbers, the budgets and the reopened file.

Benchmark on a 32-thread desktop (Ryzen 9 7950X):

  • A million instances: placed in 13–16 ms (scattered by area, then a matrix each). The viewport orbits them at 11.4 ms a frame at the median (14.1 ms at the 95th percentile): small ones become depth-tested splats, near ones their triangles, binned into tiles across the threads.
  • Field programs: 1M points x 42 instructions take 4.7 ms in the VM on one core, 2.0 ms compiled (AVX), and 0.3 ms compiled on all cores.
  • Procedural walkthrough: 1.5 s end to end. That covers a 200 x 200 terrain with 200k erosion droplets and 401 rocks and plants (0.26 s), the rail, the meadow, the save and a 960x540 render.

Added

  • The Node Editor area: the active material's shader graph as boxes, sockets and wires. Shift+A adds a node at the pointer; header drags move nodes; socket drags link, pick up and unplug links and drive the Material Output; value drags edit numbers, choices and images; X deletes; middle or empty-space drags pan, Home fits. Positions are kept in the material (saved and undone with it); unplaced nodes are laid out by depth.
  • Shader graph links may go either way: the graph keeps itself in evaluation order and refuses loops (material.link). New operators material.node_delete, material.node_move; BeeScript nodeinfo.
  • Geometry nodes: — Modifier: a Geometry Nodes modifier runs a node tree on the mesh below it. — Nodes: 15 geometry nodes (primitives, transform, join, set position, extrude, subdivide, boolean, merge by distance) and 10 field nodes (position, normal, index, value, combine / separate XYZ, math, vector math, noise, random). — Field VM: fields compile to programs for a block-vectorized SSE VM run across the job threads. — Storage: trees are saved in .bee files (NTRE) and undo with the scene. — Editing: the node editor shows the active object's tree (Tab: its material). Operators tree.*; BeeScript gtree, gnode, glink, gset, ginfo.
  • Node groups: a Group node runs another tree (geometry, value and vector through its Group Input; fields cross the boundary; 8 levels deep). Shift-click and Ctrl+G make one from the selection (tree.group), Tab goes into a group and back.
  • Scattering and instancing: — Distribute Points on Faces: by area and density, with a seed. An optional minimum distance thins the points, and the points keep their faces' normals. — Instance on Points: places a geometry at every point, aligned to the normal or up, turned at random, scaled by a field. Instances stay instances (a prototype and a matrix each) until Realize Instances. — Viewport: draws instances without realizing them. Instances under 3 px become depth-tested squares, the others their front faces, binned into tiles. A million are placed in ~12 ms and orbit at ~35 ms a frame on 32 threads. — Path tracer: takes instances as triangles, up to 4 million. — BeeScript: instances().
  • Curves: — Objects: Bezier and poly splines (Create > Bezier Curve / Bezier Circle / Path, curve.add) with a resolution per span and, per point, a radius, a tilt and a handle type (auto, aligned, vector, free). A curve object's mesh is what the curve makes, so modifiers, materials, rendering and export work on it unchanged. — Sweeps: a bevel radius and sides (with caps) or a profile curve sweep it into a mesh. Frames are parallel transported from the world up, a closed path's twist is spread over it, and tilt turns them. — Curve edit mode (Tab): click / Shift-click selection of points and handles, G / R / S, E extrude, Ctrl+click to add a point, W subdivide (the shape kept), X delete, V handle type, Alt+C cyclic. — Operators: curve.* (add, set, point, spline, select, move, extrude, subdivide, delete, cyclic, handle, tilt, radius, to_mesh). BeeScript: curve, cpoints, cpos, clength. — Files: curves are saved in .bee files (CURV). OBJ export writes bare curves as l lines, and import reads them back as 2-point polygons. — Curve nodes: Curve Line, Curve Circle, Curve to Mesh (a profile curve or a round tube), Resample Curve, Trim Curve, Fillet Curve and Curve to Points (upright point normals for instancing). In geometry nodes a curve is a chain of 2-point polygons. — The node editor's Shift+A menu wraps into columns.
  • Procedural generators: — Terrain nodes: - Terrain is a heightfield grid from octaves of Perlin noise, smooth (fBm) or ridged, mixed. - Terrace sets flat steps with smooth risers. - Erosion is hydraulic erosion by droplets that carry sediment down slopes and drop it where they slow, through a brush, deterministic per seed; 100k droplets on a 64 x 64 grid take ~75 ms. — L-systems: BeeScript lsystem(name, axiom, rules, iterations, angle [, step, radius]) rewrites the axiom by rules. A 3D turtle (F f + - & ^ \ / | [ ] !) draws lines, or tubes that thin with every branch. The L-System node has plant, bush, tree and Koch island presets. — Wave function collapse: wfc(name, nx, nz, layers, seed, "tiles") fills a 2D or 3D grid with tile objects in four turns. Which tiles may touch comes from the vertices on their faces, with no rules to write. A contradiction restarts with the next seed.
  • A template JIT for field programs: a program run over 1024 or more points is compiled to x86-64 at run time from code templates, with AVX (8 lanes) or SSE (4 lanes), and cached. 1M points x 42 instructions take ~2 ms on one core instead of ~4.7 ms in the VM. BEEMODEL_JIT=0 / =sse choose the path. --selftest runs 150 random programs through the VM and both paths and compares every output bit.
  • The procedural co-pilot (MCP): — Tools: node_types lists the node catalogue (sockets, values, choices, defaults). describe_graph and the bee://graphs resource give trees as JSON. — Proposals: propose_begin / propose_end / proposal_status let an agent build a node setup the user previews in the viewport. A banner offers Accept (Enter) and Revert (Esc); the proposal is one undo step either way. — Prompt: the MCP prompt procedural gives an agent this flow for a goal.
  • Assets: tree.save_asset (with the groups the tree runs) and material.save_asset write to ~/BeeModel/assets; asset.load adds one to any scene, asset.list lists them; the Asset Browser area adds one with a click.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.8.0
entry.summary: Phase 7 of the masterplan, "Sculpting, texturing & UV". BeeModel sculpts dense meshes and paints them:
entry.content:
• Sculpting: a sculpt mode for meshes of tens of millions of vertices, with eleven brushes, pen pressure, a stabilizer, dynamic topology and multiresolution levels.
  • UVs: seams, LSCM unwrapping, smart projection, packing and a UV editor with a distortion heat map.
  • Painting: texture painting through the UVs (in the viewport and the UV editor) on layers, and vertex colours.
  • Baking: normal, ambient occlusion and curvature maps from a high-poly mesh to a low-poly one with the path tracer's BVH, and a normalmap shader node that uses them.

The exit checks:

  • **tests/sculpt20m.py** sculpts a 25.2M-vertex mesh in the window with four strokes.
  • **tests/sculpt_paint.bees** sculpts a creature head and bakes it into a light head's maps. It then paints the light head on two layers, gives a pedestal vertex colours, saves everything to one .bee file and renders it. tests/sculpt_paint.py checks every step and the reopened file.

Benchmark on a 32-thread desktop (Ryzen 9 7950X):

  • Strokes at 60 fps on 25.2M vertices: frames that place brush dabs (brush work plus drawing) take 11.2 ms at the median and 15.8–16.4 ms at the 95th percentile, under the 16.7 ms of 60 fps. Frames in between take 2.3 ms to draw. During a stroke only the BVH leaves the brush changed are projected again, and only the screen tiles they cover (where they were and where they are) are drawn again.
  • Memory: the mesh as BeeModel keeps it takes 2.76 GB, and the whole process while sculpting takes 2.82 GB (1.02×). The peak, while entering sculpt mode, is 3.6 GB (1.3×). Measured against the bare data (positions plus quad indices, 672 MB) the process takes 4.2×: the general mesh format's per-loop data is most of it, and slimming it is future work.
  • Sculpt and paint walkthrough: 5.5 s end to end. That covers ten strokes on 127k vertices, 1024² normal, AO and curvature maps in 0.75 s together, 288 paint dabs, the save and a 960×540 render.

Added

  • Sculpt mode (Ctrl+Tab): — Structure: BVH leaves of about a thousand triangles, per-vertex normals, and undo steps that store only the moved vertices. — Brushes: draw, clay strips, crease, inflate, grab, snake hook, smooth, flatten, pinch, layer and mask; X symmetry. — Drawing: cached splat records per leaf, drawn in parallel screen tiles. During a stroke each leaf keeps its splat density, and only the tiles of the changed leaves are drawn again; the rest comes from a copy of the last frame. — Input: tablet pressure (strength / radius, three curves), the eraser end and a stroke stabilizer. — Dynamic topology (Ctrl+D): longest-edge splits and safe collapses to a detail size in pixels. — Multiresolution: per-level displacements, sculpting at any level, propagation to coarser levels, saved in .bee files. — BeeScript: sculpt, frames, frametime (frametime(k, 1): a frame's brush work).
  • UV maps: — Seams: marked or from sharp edges. — Unwrapping: least squares conformal maps (own sparse CG solver) and smart projection, with islands packed into the unit square. — UV editor: island selection, move / scale / rotate, and an area / angle distortion heat map. — Files: OBJ vt and glTF TEXCOORD_0.
  • Textures through UVs in the material preview and the path tracer; image.new; images saved inside .bee files as PNG.
  • Texture painting (Shift+Tab): — Strokes: projected viewport strokes that paint only what is visible, plus strokes in the UV editor, with an undo history. — Layers: opacity, normal / multiply / add blending and visibility, with the stack saved in .bee files.
  • Vertex colours (Shift+V): — Shading: per triangle in solid view, smooth in the preview and the path tracer. — Files: OBJ v x y z r g b, glTF COLOR_0 and .bee.
  • Baking (object.bake, bake(...)): — Maps: tangent-space normal maps, ambient occlusion (48 rays) and curvature. — Method: a cage distance and dilated island borders. A bake is one texture-paint undo step.
  • A normalmap shader node: a tangent-space normal map (as baking writes it) tilts the shading normal in the preview and the path tracer.
  • tests/sculpt20m.py and tests/sculpt_paint.py in CI.

Fixed

  • Drawing a mesh of more than ~45M triangles in object mode overflowed the rasterizer's triangle buffer (a 32-bit size) and crashed. Huge meshes now draw the triangles that fit in half the frame arena.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.7.0
entry.summary: Phase 6 of the masterplan, "CAD & digital fabrication". BeeModel designs parts to make:
entry.content:
• Parametric parts: parameters with units drive constrained sketches.
  • Features: pads, pockets, holes, shells, fillets and patterns, in a tree that rebuilds whenever anything changes.
  • Implicit shapes: signed-distance blends and lattices.
  • Output: 3MF for printers, DXF / SVG of sketches, and PDF drawings.

The exit check, tests/enclosure.bees, designs an electronics enclosure from dimensioned sketches: a filleted, shelled case with a cable hole, and a lid with a fitted lip and vents. All dimensions are parameters. Changing the width (80 to 100 mm) rebuilds everything, and both 3MF files are read by lib3mf in strict mode and sliced by PrusaSlicer in CI.

Benchmark on a 32-thread desktop:

  • Enclosure: both bodies (10 features) are built, rebuilt after the parameter change and exported twice as 3MF plus a PDF drawing in 0.65 s in total.
  • Gyroid lattice: a 96-cell mesh (250k triangles) in 0.1 s.
  • Gyroid infill: an infill for a 60 × 40 × 30 mm shelled box in 0.3 s.

Added

  • The feature tree: — Features: pad (symmetric / reverse), pocket (through / reverse / symmetric), revolve (full or partial), hole (at a sketch's loose points), shell (open top or bottom), fillet and chamfer with edge selectors (all / vertical / horizontal / top / bottom), linear and circular patterns, and infill. — How it works: features live in the CAD document (undo, .bee) and refer to bodies and sketches by persistent object ids. The tree replays in order with exact booleans and bevels after any change. — Values and status: values may be expressions. Each feature reports a status (ok, missing sketch, no profile, geometry failed, ...), and a feature that would open a closed body fails without changing it. — Where to see it: Properties and scene_summary. — BeeScript: pad pocket revolve hole shell fillet chamfer pattern infill feature features fstatus.
  • Profiles from sketches (prof.s): — Loops: closed loops with welded ends, arcs and circles tessellated, and even-odd nesting into material and holes. — Caps: ear clipping with hole bridging (n-gon caps when there is no hole). — Solids: prisms, revolutions and inward offsets.
  • Measurement and mass properties: — Tool: the measure tool (Shift+M) snaps to vertices or the surface and gives the distance with its components, and the angle at a middle point. — Mass properties: area, volume, centre of mass and mass, from a new per-material density (g/cm^3), in world space and scene units. — Reporting: object.measure sends them to the console, the status bar and agents. — BeeScript: area mass centroid fangle measurement.
  • The SDF / F-rep kernel (sdf.s): — Shapes: sphere, box (rounded), cylinder, torus, and gyroid and strut-grid lattices. — Operations: smooth union, subtraction and intersection, shells, moves and turns, and extruded profiles. — Meshing: the field is sampled on all threads and meshed by marching tetrahedra, so the result is always closed and manifold. — BeeScript: ssphere sbox scyl storus sgyroid sgrid sunion ssub sisect sshell smove srot sdist smesh sclear.
  • Fabrication output: — 3MF: a zip written by our own code (deflate, CRC-32) with every mesh in millimetres, Z up. — DXF and SVG of a sketch (construction geometry on its own layer or dashed). — PDF drawings: front, top and right views in third-angle projection with hidden lines dashed (a depth buffer per view), sharp and silhouette edges, overall dimensions and a title block, written by hand with an exact xref.
  • Printability: — Wall thickness: measured per face with rays through a triangle grid. View › Show Thin Walls colours faces under the minimum red and under twice it yellow. — Print check: mesh.print_check reports whether the part is closed, the thinnest wall, the overhang area (excluding the bed) and the size. — BeeScript: thinnest().
  • tests/enclosure.py: the walkthrough, checked by our own 3MF reader, by lib3mf (strict) and by PrusaSlicer. It runs in CI and in ci/local.sh.
  • Sketches with a constraint solver: — Sketch objects: a new object type on the XY, XZ or YZ plane (with an offset), placed by the object's transform. It holds points, lines, circles and arcs in a copy-on-write block that undo shares. — Constraints: coincident, horizontal, vertical, parallel, perpendicular, equal, tangent, fixed, distance (also horizontal / vertical), length, radius, diameter, angle, point on line / circle, midpoint and symmetric. Dimensions may be expressions, so parameters drive them. — Solver: damped Gauss-Newton (Levenberg-Marquardt) in doubles, one connected group of unknowns at a time. The Jacobian's rank gives the degrees of freedom left and which points and entities are fully constrained. Equations that stay unsatisfied are conflicts. — Sketch mode (Tab): - tools: L lines (chains reuse points and level / plumb segments become horizontal / vertical), O circles, R rectangles; - click to select, drag points as the sketch solves; - constraint keys C H V E P N T F M, D for a dimension typed on the command line (expressions too), X to delete; - entities coloured by status, constraint labels, and a status line with the DOF. — Scripts and files: - BeeScript sketch, point, line, circle, arc, rect, pt, con, dof, conflicts, sx, sy, sr, skinfo; - sketches re-solve when parameters or units change; - saved in .bee (SKCH); - shown in Properties and to agents in scene_summary.
  • Parameters, expressions and scene units, the base of the CAD phase: — Units: scene.units mm|cm|m|in sets what one scene unit is (metres by default). — Expressions: + - * / ^, parentheses, units (mm cm m in ft for lengths in scene units, deg rad for angles), pi, e, and sin cos tan asin acos atan sqrt abs floor ceil round min max. — Parameters: param.set <name> <expression> (for example width = 10*wall + 2mm), param.remove, param.list. Values are evaluated on demand and cached. A cycle, a syntax error or an unknown name is refused, and the scene keeps its last good state. — Where they live: parameters belong to a copy-on-write CAD document that undo shares, like the materials, and that is saved in .bee (CADD chunk). Properties lists them with their values. — Scripts and agents: BeeScript param(name [, expression]) and expr(text); scene_summary shows the units and the parameters.

Changed

  • Booleans: — Edge points: a point within 1e-7 of an edge's length splits it in the triangulation. A constraint through a vertex is split there. — Classification: rays walk a grid of triangles, so large meshes classify in milliseconds. Flat triangles are not crossed. — Capacity: room for more intersection segments.
  • Feature booleans clean their result: vertices closer than 1e-4 of the size are welded and flat triangles go into their neighbours, so chains of booleans stay robust.
  • mesh_finish fans skip flat ears, so polygons with corners in a line triangulate without zero-area triangles.
  • Bevels: — partial edge sets with several segments are manifold; — the faces at a rounded edge's ends take the arc; — rounded edges meeting at a corner share it.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.6.0
entry.summary: Phase 5 of the masterplan, "Materials & rendering". BeeModel renders:
entry.content:
• Materials: principled materials, optionally with shader graphs.
  • Hive: a CPU path tracer with a denoiser and HDRI lighting.
  • Render window: stays interactive while it refines.
  • Files: readers and writers for the usual image formats, and glTF.

A product-shot benchmark runs in CI. It renders a studio scene (car paint, gold, glass, a light strip, a noise-bumped plinth) to convergence: 32 samples plus the denoiser stay within 4.5 levels RMS of a 512-sample reference. At 1920 × 1080 that takes about 5 s on 32 threads (the budget is 10 s, scaled to the runner's cores). The same scene also renders at 1080p in the Render area while the viewport is orbited, with a median frame time of about 15 ms.

Added

  • The product-shot scene (tests/product_shot.bees) and its benchmark (fakewl product_shot).
  • The render's resolve (tone mapping into the Render area) runs on all cores and only redoes the rows that have new samples. While a 1080p render runs, frames take about 15 ms on 4 threads.
  • glTF 2.0 and MTL: — Export: file.export_gltf <path> writes .glb (binary chunks) or .gltf (base64 buffer). Mesh objects become nodes with translation, a quaternion from our Euler angles, and scale, plus u32 triangles and positions with bounds. Materials become metallic-roughness PBR with emission (KHR_materials_emissive_strength above 1), transmission, IOR and clearcoat. Blender reads the files. — Import: file.import_gltf <path> reads .glb and .gltf with embedded, data: or external buffers. It walks the default scene's node tree (TRS or matrices) and bakes each triangle primitive's world transform into a new object. Equal positions are welded, so meshes stay connected, and materials map back with their extensions. — MTL with OBJ: OBJ import reads mtllib and assigns the first usemtl. The MTL reader handles Kd, Ke, Ni, d / Tr, Ns (to roughness), Tf, the PBR keys Pr / Pm / Pc / Pcr and map_Kd (the image becomes the base colour).
  • Shader graphs: a material can hold up to 12 nodes. — Nodes: image, noise (Perlin fBm), checker, gradient, mix (mix / add / multiply / subtract / screen), colour ramp, math (ten operations) and bump. — Sockets: nodes drive the base colour, metallic, roughness, emission and the normal. — Evaluation: Hive and the material preview evaluate graphs per shading point. Coordinates are object space, or the box projection for images. Bump re-evaluates the graph a little along the triangle's edges and tilts the normal (Blinn). — Safety: links only point to earlier nodes, so graphs cannot loop. — Editing: - BeeScript node, link, nodeset, socket; - operators material.node / link / node_set / socket / nodes_clear; - every change is undoable. — Agents: scene_summary shows each graph (nodes, values, inputs, links, sockets). — Files: graphs are saved in .bee (MGRF; damaged graphs are cleared). — Textures: material.texture now builds a one-node graph. — Records: material records are now 1 KiB in memory. The MATS chunk keeps its 128-byte records, so 0.5 files still open.
  • Image textures and an HDRI world: — Textures: material.texture <material> <image|none> [size] gives a material a base-colour image. Until UVs arrive it is box-projected in object space (per face, by its normal) and sampled bilinearly and repeating, with 8-bit images decoded from sRGB. Hive and the material preview both show it. — HDRI world: world.hdri <image|none>, world.strength, world.rotation light the scene with an equirectangular image instead of the studio sky and sun. - Hive importance-samples the HDRI through a 2D CDF (luminance × sin θ) with MIS. In a flat HDRI a white diffuse sphere vanishes (the white-furnace test). - The material preview takes irradiance from 9 spherical-harmonic coefficients and reflections from a blurred copy, and turns off its softboxes. — Files: .bee keeps the image paths (IMGS, reloaded in order; missing files keep their place) and the world (WRLD). — Agents: scene_summary lists the images, each material's texture and the world.
  • Image files, all with our own code: — inflate: stored, fixed and dynamic Huffman blocks, with a 10-bit lookup table. — PNG reader: every colour type and bit depth, all five filters, Adam7 interlacing and tRNS. — JPEG decoder: baseline (SOF0/1), any chroma subsampling, restart markers, SSE float IDCT, libjpeg-style fancy upsampling. It matches Pillow to within 3 levels. — Radiance HDR reader: RGBE, RLE or flat, top-down or bottom-up. — OpenEXR writer: half floats, ZIP blocks (predictor + deflate). oiiotool reads the files. — Commands: image.load / image.save (PNG or EXR); render.save <path>.exr writes linear passes. — BeeScript: image(path), imgsize, imgpixel. — Agents: image commands need file access. — Tests: tests/image_io.py checks 30 PNG variants exactly, eight JPEG kinds against Pillow, HDR exactly and EXR round trips.
  • A denoiser for Hive renders: an edge-avoiding à-trous wavelet filter (after Dammertz et al. and SVGF): — Guides: the albedo, normal and depth passes. It filters the lighting only (radiance ÷ albedo), so colours and edges stay sharp. — Strength: set by the noise. A per-pixel variance comes from the luminance moments of the samples, so converged renders pass through almost unchanged. — Results: 16 samples + denoise get about as close to the reference as 256 samples. 1080p denoises in about 50 ms. — Where: Render › Denoise (render.denoise, on by default, saved in .bee) denoises a render when it finishes or is stopped; render.image <path> w h spp 1 and render(path, w, h, spp, 1) too.
  • The Render window: — F12 (Render › Render) starts a progressive render in a Render area beside the viewport, opening the area if needed. The main loop spends about 14 ms of each turn on more samples, in bands of rows, so the UI stays live at any resolution. Esc (or Render › Stop) stops it. — Status line: size, samples so far, time and the shown pass. — Passes: albedo, normal and depth from the first hit, next to the beauty pass. render.pass switches between them, and render.save <path> [pass] writes any of them as PNG. — Settings: render.settings <w> <h> <samples> (default 960 × 540 × 128), saved in .bee (RNDR chunk). — Agents can start, stop and inspect renders with edit access; saving needs file access. — Editor type: Render is a new editor type (area.type_render).
  • Materials with principled parameters: — base colour, metallic, roughness, specular, IOR; — transmission; — emission and its strength; — clearcoat and its roughness; — alpha. Where they appear: — Scene: one material table, shared with undo (copy-on-write), and a per-object assignment. — Properties › Material: + New, drag the name to pick another material, drag values, x to remove. — Viewport: solid shading shows the base colour. — Files: saved in .bee (MATS and OMAT chunks) and exported as MTL with OBJ. — Scripts and agents: BeeScript material, matset, matget, assign, matof; the material.new / assign / set / remove operators; materials in scene_summary.
  • Hive, a path tracer (CPU, all cores): — Scene and BVH: a world-space triangle soup with auto-smoothed normals, and a binned-SAH BVH collapsed to 4-wide nodes traversed with SSE. — Light transport: path tracing with next-event estimation and multiple importance sampling over the studio sky (cosine), a sun disc, light objects (points) and emissive triangles (area × power). — Materials: the principled BSDF covers Lambert, GGX reflection (metallic workflow), rough dielectric transmission with Fresnel and total internal reflection, and clearcoat. — Sampling: Russian roulette and a firefly clamp. — Output: progressive passes into a float buffer, ACES resolve, render.image and BeeScript render(). Agents need file access to render. — Tests: a white-furnace energy check, a convergence check and a time budget.
  • Material preview, a viewport mode (View › Material Preview, Shift+Z): — every pixel is shaded with its object's principled material (Lambert + GGX specular with Fresnel, clearcoat, approximate transmission, emission); — lighting is a studio environment (sky / ground, split-sum approximation) plus three softbox lights, then ACES tone mapping; — the rasterizer now keeps a visibility buffer (the triangle of each pixel), and the shading pass works from it; — per-corner normals smooth faces closer than 30°, so cubes stay sharp and spheres look round; — a 300k-triangle scene orbits in about 6 ms on 32 threads, with a CI budget.

Changed

  • The screenshot moved from F12 to Shift+F12; F12 now renders.

Fixed

  • Hive's table of its own mappings had room for 8 entries but accepted 16. Renders that needed a ninth buffer (the denoiser's, a file's) could overwrite the variables after it.
  • Hive's per-triangle texture data (box UVs) were not reordered with the BVH's leaf order, so textures on multi-triangle meshes came out scrambled. The object-space data that replaces them is reordered.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.5.0
entry.summary: Phase 4 of the masterplan, "Polygon modeling". BeeModel becomes a modeler: edit mode with the usual tools, adjustable last operations, a modifier stack, robust booleans, and mesh analysis and repair. A hard-surface walkthrough runs in CI on every change. It builds a part from the keyboard and the menus: 1. a pocket (inset, extrude); 2. a through hole (boolean); 3. rounded edges (Bevel modifier). It checks that the part is closed, then saves, reopens and exports it.
entry.content:
Added

  • Edit mode (Tab) for mesh objects: — vertex, edge and face select modes (1 / 2 / 3); — click, Shift+click, select all / none (A), invert (Ctrl+I), box select (B, Ctrl subtracts), edge loops (Alt+click) and select linked (Ctrl+L); — G / R / S on the selection, with axis constraints, snapping, typed values and gizmos; — overlays (edges, vertex dots, face dots, a tint on selected faces) that are depth tested against the rasterizer's depth buffer, so hidden elements are neither drawn nor picked. Geometry is copy-on-write, so undo snapshots keep the previous mesh.
  • BeeScript mesh functions: edit, verts, edges, faces, vpos, selected, vsel, vselect, volume.
  • Mesh operators (edit mode, Mesh menu). Each one is a single undo step. — Building: extrude region (E, slides along the normal), extrude edges, extrude individual faces (Alt+E), inset (I), duplicate (Shift+D), subdivide. — Removing: delete vertices / edges / faces (X), dissolve into n-gons (Ctrl+X). — Merging: at center (M), collapse, by distance. — Faces and normals: fill / make face (F), flip normals, recalculate normals (Shift+N, consistent and outwards). Scripts and agents pass the distance as the operator argument.
  • More modeling tools: — loop cut (Ctrl+R): a hover preview, the wheel sets the number of cuts; scripts pass an edge and a count; — bevel (Ctrl+B): the width is dragged or typed, the wheel adds segments for round profiles, and corner patches close the gaps where beveled edges meet; — knife (K) for cuts through the visible faces, and bisect for a plane cut; both use one plane-cut core; — bridge edge loops between two boundary loops; — spin, which sweeps a profile around the 3D cursor (steps, angle, axis).
  • Modifier stack: Mirror, Array, Solidify, Subdivision Surface, Bevel, Decimate and Remesh. — Non-destructive and cached per object. — Edited in the Properties editor (add, toggle, reorder, apply, remove, drag values); undoable. — Saved in .bee files (MODS chunk). — Scriptable: modifier, modset, modapply, modremove, modcount, everts, efaces. — Shown to agents in scene_summary. Subdivision is a parallel Catmull–Clark with cached topology. On a 102,400-quad mesh, level 3 (6.5 M faces) builds in about 125 ms, and an edit updates it in about 19 ms.
  • BeeScript: vmove (move a vertex) and clock().
  • Mesh booleans: union, difference and intersection that stay exact on degenerate input (faces on faces, edges on edges, identical meshes, angles typed to six decimals). — Edit › Boolean Union / Difference / Intersect and object.boolean union|difference|intersect [keep] combine the active mesh with another selected one, as one undo step. — A Boolean modifier reads another object's mesh and follows it when that object moves; it is saved in .bee files. — BeeScript boolean(a, b, kind) and manifold(name). — Exact integer predicates with a symbolic perturbation. Faces lying on each other resolve as expected: a flush cut goes through, touching solids fuse, and A − A is empty. — A stress corpus runs in CI. It checks the volume identities and closed results on 300 cases (general position, coincident and identical operands). A sphere with 63k triangles minus one with 16k takes about 40 ms.
  • Performance budgets for the modeling core run in CI (tests/perf_modeling.bees). The local times are: | Operation | Size | Time | |---|---|---| | Subdivision build | 508k faces | ~11 ms | | Subdivision update | same mesh | ~1 ms | | Analysis | 127k faces | ~10 ms | | Repair | 127k faces | ~75 ms | | Boolean | 254k triangles | ~170 ms |
  • Redo panel: adjust the last operation. Extrude, individual extrude, inset, bevel, loop cut, merge by distance and spin report their values. Drag or scroll a value, use F9 to type, or call edit.redo_last "values" (also for agents): the operator runs again from its undo snapshot and stays one undo step.
  • 3D cursor: Shift+right click places it on the surface or the ground; new objects are created there. View › Reset 3D Cursor puts it back.
  • Keys can depend on the mode (operator flags OPF_EDIT / OPF_OBJECT): X, A, F and Shift+D mean the mesh versions in edit mode. Home resets the camera in either mode.
  • Mesh analysis and repair. — Overlays for the active mesh (View › Show …), with counts in the viewport: - face normals; - non-manifold edges (more than two faces, or two facing the same way); - boundary edges; - degenerate faces; - overhangs (faces facing down steeper than 45°, or a given angle). — Edit › Repair Mesh (mesh.repair [distance]), in object or edit mode, as one undo step. It merges by distance, removes degenerate and duplicate faces, fills holes, makes the normals consistent and outward, and drops loose vertices, then reports what it changed. — BeeScript analyze(name, what) for scripts and agents.

Changed

  • Meshes store a vertex selection and a triangle-to-polygon map.

Fixed

  • Cylinder and cone caps and the whole torus were wound inwards, and the plane and grid faced down. All primitives now face out (up).
  • Bevel (the tool and the modifier) is fixed for widths larger than nearby edges, such as around a hole cut by a boolean, where thin triangles meet the beveled edge: — offsets are clamped so neighbouring corner points never cross; — the strips across beveled edges are oriented from the topology, not from their shape. The result stays closed.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.4.0
entry.summary: Phase 3 of the masterplan, "AI-native layer": AI agents become first-class users of BeeModel. They can see, script and edit the scene, under permissions the user controls, and the user can revert their changes.
entry.content:
Added

  • MCP server for AI agents. The running app listens on $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/beemodel.sock, and beemodel --mcp-bridge connects Claude Code / Claude Desktop over stdio. Tools: scene_summary, create_primitive, set_transform, select, delete, run_operator, undo, redo, plus every agent-safe operator as op_<id>. Resource: bee://scene. Agent edits are undoable and echoed in the console.
  • viewport_capture MCP tool. The UI is rendered off-screen, so the image shows the scene right after the agent's last edit. The tool returns an MCP image block holding the viewport (or the whole window) as a PNG.
  • BeeScript, a scripting language compiled in one pass to bytecode for a stack VM. It has numbers with units (2m, 45deg), texts, variables, if, while, for i in 0..n, functions and recursion, plus scene, math and text builtins. Reference: docs/BEESCRIPT.md. — Console lines that are not operator ids run as BeeScript, with REPL-style echo; variables and functions persist between lines. — A script run is one undo step: undo now supports grouped changes. — Macro recording (Edit → Record Macro) saves operators, selection clicks and G/R/S results as BeeScript in ~/BeeModel/scripts/macro.bees; script.run plays a macro or any .bees file back. — script_eval MCP tool. Agent scripts may only run agent-safe operators. — beemodel --eval 'code' / --run file.bees run scripts without a window.
  • Safe agent edits: — Permission tiers (read-only / edit / files), set in the new AI menu and enforced for every tool, run_operator and script_eval. The default is edit, so file access must be granted by the user. The status bar shows the tier and how many agents are connected. — Change sets. Each agent request is one undo step, labeled Agent: <tool>. Undo steps now keep their own copy of the label. — AI Activity editor (AI → AI Activity Pane, or any area's editor menu). It lists recent agent calls and has a one-click Revert last agent change button (agent.revert).
  • Own JSON reader / writer, with a strict RFC 8259 validator for incoming messages.
  • MCP conformance suite in CI. It drives a full session through --mcp-bridge like Claude Code does, and checks: — tool schemas and the result shape of every curated tool; — JSON-RPC error codes (-32700 / -32600 / -32601); — id echo, split writes and 60 KiB requests; — UTF-8 round trips and concurrent clients.
  • docs/MCP.md: connecting Claude Code / Claude Desktop, and the tools, permissions and protocol details.

Changed

  • --list-ops no longer truncates long descriptions.
  • PNG files are now compressed. The encoder picks a Sub or Up filter per row and then deflates the data (LZ77 plus fixed Huffman codes). A 1280×800 screenshot drops from about 3 MB to about 150 KB.
  • .bss is excluded from transparent huge pages, so the large, mostly idle script buffers cost no memory until they are used.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.3.0
entry.summary: Phase 2 of the masterplan, "Scene, viewport & files": BeeModel becomes a small but real 3D editor.
entry.content:
Added

  • Scene with real objects: a Blender-like default scene (Camera, Light, Cube); objects have a name, location, rotation, scale and a mesh.
  • Polygon meshes with n-gons, derived edges and triangles; primitives: cube, plane, grid, UV sphere, cylinder, cone, torus.
  • Selection: click in the viewport or the outliner (Shift extends), A to select all / none; X / Delete removes, Shift+D duplicates (unique names like Cube.001).
  • The outliner lists the scene's objects and scrolls; Properties shows the active object's transform and mesh statistics.
  • Solid shading: a multithreaded tile rasterizer (parallel setup, binning and rasterization, SSE 4-pixel edge functions, depth and object-ID buffers) with Blender-style selection outlines. About 1.2 M triangles render in 8–9 ms at 1280×800 on 32 threads, with output identical for any thread count. Z toggles wireframe.
  • Exact click picking from the ID buffer.
  • Modal transforms like Blender's: G / R / S with X/Y/Z constraints, Ctrl snapping (1 m, 15°, 0.1), typed values, Enter / LMB to confirm and Esc / RMB to cancel. Move / Rotate / Scale tool gizmos can be dragged.
  • Undo / redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) for create, delete, duplicate and transforms. Snapshots share reference-counted meshes; the history is bounded (256 steps / 64 MiB). Edit › Undo History lists the steps.
  • Files: native .bee save / open (chunked, atomic writes, validated on load), OBJ import / export, STL import (binary + ASCII, welded) / export, PNG screenshots (F12), autosave every 25 changes, file.recover. The title bar shows the current file.
  • Operators accept a text argument from the command line (file.save ~/x.bee); without one, the command line opens pre-filled.
  • Shift+D shares the mesh with the original (copy-on-write arrives with edit mode), so duplicates cost almost no memory.

Fixed

  • Keymap parser: the word "aliases" inside the keycodes section name was taken for an alias statement, which swallowed the Escape and 1 keys (& on AZERTY). Digits now all type correctly.

Changed

  • G, R and S now start transforms (Blender layout). The grid toggle moved to Shift+G, and the tools to Shift+Q / W / E / R.
  • Binary size budget raised from 64 KiB to 256 KiB (now ~67 KB); the masterplan target remains < 2 MB for v1.0.
  • Arenas keep memory that is in use resident instead of releasing it every frame (released after sustained low use).

entry.title: BeeModel 0.2.0
entry.summary: Phase 1 of the masterplan, "Foundations": the runtime every modeling feature will build on.
entry.content:
Added

  • Operator spine: every action is declared once with the OPERATOR macro and collected by the linker into one table. Menus, tool buttons, check marks, shortcut labels and the keymap are all driven by it.
  • --list-ops prints every operator (id, key binding, label, description).
  • New key bindings: T (tools pane), N (outliner pane), F1 (shortcut list in the console), Ctrl+N/O/S/Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z.
  • docs/ARCHITECTURE.md: modules, calling convention, how to add an operator.
  • Real keyboard support without libxkbcommon: the XKB keymap sent by the compositor is parsed in assembly. Shift / Caps Lock / AltGr levels and dead keys (accents) work for any layout.
  • Layout-aware shortcuts: bindings follow the key label, so Ctrl+Z is Undo on AZERTY and QWERTZ keyboards too.
  • Key repeat using the compositor's rate and delay (timerfd).
  • Console command line: a UTF-8 text field with caret, selection (Shift, Ctrl+A), history (Up/Down) and Tab completion of operator ids. Enter runs any operator by id.
  • New operators: console.focus (Enter), console.clear (Ctrl+L), console.list_ops.
  • TrueType text, with no FreeType: our own TrueType parser (cmap 4/12, composite glyphs), an anti-aliased signed-area rasterizer, a glyph cache and alpha blending. The UI uses a proportional sans font and the console a monospace font, both loaded from the system (Noto / DejaVu / Liberation).
  • Full Unicode text (UTF-8): accented and international characters display correctly. BEEMODEL_FONT / BEEMODEL_MONO_FONT select fonts; none keeps the bitmap font.
  • HiDPI / fractional scaling (wp_fractional_scale_v1 + wp_viewporter): the UI renders natively at 125%, 150%, 200% and other scales, with crisp text and geometry instead of compositor upscaling.
  • Job system: worker threads on every core (raw clone + futex, 0% CPU when idle) and parallel_for with atomic chunk claiming; the viewport background is already filled in parallel. BEEMODEL_THREADS limits the thread count.
  • Memory: bump arenas (per frame and per thread, giving memory back to the kernel after spikes) and pools with generational handles.
  • --selftest: built-in tests for the allocators and the job system, plus a benchmark (12× faster with 32 threads on the reference machine). Runs in CI.
  • Area system like Blender's: the window is a tree of resizable areas. Each area has a header to switch its editor (3D Viewport, Tools, Outliner, Properties, Console) and to maximize (Ctrl+Space), split side by side or top/bottom, or close it. Each viewport has its own camera.
  • Command palette (F3): fuzzy search over every command, showing its id and shortcut. Up/Down select, Enter runs.

Changed

  • Tools / Outliner / Console toggles (T, N, View menu) now add and remove areas; the Properties pane is now its own area.

Testing

  • Golden-image regression tests (pixel diff against tests/golden).
  • Performance and memory budgets checked in CI: first frame in about 4 ms, median input-to-frame latency about 0.6 ms at 1280×800, about 2.3 MiB of private memory.

Changed

  • Source split into separate modules (object files) with explicit exports.
  • Help › Keyboard Shortcuts is generated from the operator table.
  • Redo is now Ctrl+Shift+Z.

entry.title: BeeModel 0.1.0
entry.summary: First release: the application shell that the 3D modeling tool will be built on.
entry.content:
Added

  • Native Wayland client in pure x86-64 assembly with no libraries: raw syscalls and a hand-written wire protocol (wl_compositor, wl_shm, xdg_wm_base, wl_seat, wp_cursor_shape_v1).
  • Title bar drawn by the app: move by dragging, double-click to maximize, minimize/maximize/close buttons, edge resizing for floating windows.
  • Menu system with File, Edit, View, Create and Help dropdowns, hover switching, check marks and shortcut hints.
  • Resizable Tools, Outliner/Properties and Console panes with draggable splitters; each pane can be shown or hidden from the View menu.
  • 3D viewport canvas: orbit/pan/zoom camera, perspective projection with near-plane and Liang–Barsky clipping, ground grid, axes, orientation gizmo and a demo cube.
  • Status bar, console log, keyboard shortcuts (Q/W/E/R, G, F, Esc, Ctrl+Q).
  • --version and --help command-line flags.
  • Event-driven rendering paced by frame callbacks: 0% CPU when idle, double-buffered shared-memory framebuffer, about 60 KB of private memory.
  • build.sh, run.sh and package.sh scripts.
  • Headless test harness (fake Wayland compositor) and GitHub Actions CI and release pipelines.
